Data: Data are the collection of raw facts and figure which are unorganized, uninterpreted, and isolated, which doesn’t give any particular sense. They are randomly gathered. So that they can be processed to obtain the desired result.

Ram, 17, Pokhara, 18

Information: Information are the processed form of data. Information gives a meaning full result after data are interpreted.

Ram 17 year old and lives in Pokhara 18.

As we know, very organization from the prehistoric time deals with data and information. Data are very necessary for organization to operate. In previous time, data used to be collected randomly and were not organized in any particular order which leads to following drawbacks .

  1. Some information was stored in more than one file. (Data redundancy).
  2. Difficult to present data from the user’s view.
  3. Data security was one of the major problem.
  4. Data processing and manipulation were difficult.
  5. Data retrieval were very slow.

Hence, concept of database arise in order to overcome the above drawbacks or limitations. Database is collection of interrelated data or entities stored in tabular form. It gives very useful information for an organization during data manipulation and decision making. It provides a base for foundation for managing large volume of data in a well organized manner. Simply database is a systematic and organized form of data so that user can retrieve or access data whenever required within no time. For eg, telephone directory, dictionary, marks ledger, customer records etc.

In past people used file processing system / flat file system in order to store data and keep record due to difficulty in processing file and having following  limitations. This system are no longer in use rather people use DBMS in to order Keep record systematically, scientifically and securely.

Limitations of flat file system.

  1. Data security system is one of the major problem in flat file system.
  2. Data Sharing was almost impossible or difficult.
  3. Some record was stored in more than one file. (Data redundancy)
  4. Difficult to represent data through user prospective.
  5. It is difficult for processing complex queries.

DBMS (Database Management System)

DBMS is a computerized record keeping system. It is a software that defines, manipulates and  manage the database. It allows to access the file, update the record and retrieve data as requested. In other word, DBMS is defined as the collection of interrelated  data and set of programs to access there data. The collection of data is usually a database which contains the information about any particular organization. The primary goal of DBMS is to provide an effective and efficient environment for both data retrieval and  storing data in database. For example MS Access, Oracle, MY SQL, Fox-Pro, D-base etc

Advantages of DBMS

1) Sharing data: Using DBMS, data stored in database can be shared among multiple users or computer. For example, branches of bank share data from database.

2) Reduce data redundancy: Data redundancy refer to duplication or repetition of same data over and over. DBMS reduces such type of unnecessary repetition of data.

3) Data backup and recovery: Using DBMS, we can easily create spare copy of original files and documents that can be later used in case of accidental or intentional loss and damages.

4) Data security: Using DBMS we can restrict use of database to the unauthorized person. It helps to ensure date security.

5) Multiple user interface: DBMS facilitates sharing of data which means same data can be accessed from multiple device and location. Hence, user can experience multiple interface to access same set of data.

6) Data Integrity: Data Integrity refers to consistency of data. Using database we can arrange same sort of data in a like order. We can define and enforce constraints for data integrity.

Disadvantages of DBMS

1) Expensive: It may be expensive to run and operate DBMS for any organization.

2) Changing Technology: It is very much difficult to incorporate latest changing technology in existing system. In order to create and maintain database technical manpower and trainings are required.

3) Backup is needed: Since data maybe damage anytime accidentally or intentionally. So, it is mandatory to create a backup.

Database Model

There are different forms of Database Management system. Each characterized by the way where data are defined and structured. This arrangement of data in several structure are known as data base model. Different types of database model. Click here for full explanation with pros, cons and diagram.

Hierarchical database model

It is one of the oldest type of database model. In this model data are represented in the forms of record, each record has multiple field or attributes. All records are arranged in database as tree like structure. The relationship between the records is called parent child relationship in which one child record relates to only a single parent i.e child posses property only property of a single parent. Here child are restricted to use the property of a parent to whom it doesn't belong.

Advantages

  1. It is the simplest and the easiest model.
  2. It supports one to one or one to many relationship.
  3. Searching is easier and faster if parent is known.

Disadvantages

  1. It is an old fashion and outdated database model.
  2. It doesn’t support many to one relationship.
  3. It doesn’t reduce data redundancy because some data are written over different places.

Network database model

This network model replace hierarchical model due to some limitation on the model. Suppose an employee relates to two different department then hierarchical model cannot be able to arrange record in proper place. So, network database model was emerged to arrange non-hierarchical database. The structure of database is more like graph rather than tree structure. A network model consists of collection of record which are interrelated to each other with the help of relationship. Each records have multiple fields and each field has only one data value. In this type of model a parent may have multiple child, as well as child can have multiple parent.

Advantages

  1. It accepts many to many relationships. So, It is more flexible .
  2. It reduces data redundancy.
  3. This network mode is simple and easy to design.
  4. Searching is faster due to use of multi-directional pointer.

Disadvantages

  1. Needs long program to handle the relationship.
  2. Lack of structural independence.
  3. Less security

Relational database model

In relational database model, the data are organized into tables which contains multiple row and columns. These tables are called relations. A row in a table represents a relationship among a set of values. Since, a table is collection of such relationship. It is generally referred to the mathematical term relations from which the relational database model derives its name. It is also known as RDBMS.

Note: The database system which stores and display data in tabular format of rows and column like spreadsheet is known as RDBMS. It is the most practical DBMS those days. For example, MS-Access, MY SQL, Oracle etc

Advantages

  1. There is less data redundancy.
  2. Breaking of complex database into simple is very much easier.
  3. Database processing is faster than other model.

Disadvantage

  1. Establishing more relationships complex.
  2. It requires powerful computer and data storage device.

Centralized database VS Distributed database

Centralized database

It is a simple type which works on client server basis. In this type clients or user are directly connected to the centrally totally located server. This server hosts the data of its client or user and helps them to store and retrieve data as requirement. This type of system are used in small scale industries which doesn't have to deal with large volume of data and user. Centralized database runs on single computer which may have single or multiple user. Since database is centralized, security is not a crucial part here. The maintenance of database is easier because of data are centrally stored. This type of system denote allow unauthorized person to access data.

Advantages

  1. Suitable for small scale industries.
  2. Operation and maintenance is easier.
  3. Since it prevent unauthorized person being accessed to database, it minimizes risk factor.

Disadvantages

  1. Data are not secured in this type of system.
  2. Not suitable for large scale industries.
  3. Failure of centrally located serves will collapse whole network.

Distributed database

This type of database system are complex in structure, instead of storing and retrieving data from centrally located server, it uses several numbers of database and server randomly located at different place. It is the collection of multiple logically interrelated database which are distributed in many geographical location. Since server are located at different locations user can experience a good speed of bandwidth. Similarly, back up and recovery process is lot more easier there, which makes data more secured. This type of system is used by large organization who has to deal with large volume of data and user all around the world. Since it is distributed in nature there may arises security issue and are costly to maintain and operate. Simply, distributed database system are the collection of several number of centralized database system in different locations.

Advantages

  1. Backup and recovery of data is easier.
  2. It can handle large volume of data and user all over the word.
  3. User can experience high speed bandwidth.

Disadvantages

  1. Very expensive to operate and maintain.
  2. Data security may be real issue.

Structure query Language (SQL)

SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is an international standard data base query language for accessing and managing data in the database. SQL was introduced and developed by IBM in early 1970’s. It was able to control relational database. SQL is not a complete programming language. It is only used for communicating with database. SQL has statement for data definition (DDL), data manipulation (DML) and data control (DCL). A query is a request to a DBMS for the retrieval, modification, insertion and deletion of the data from database.

SQL is made of three sub languages: DDL, DML and DCL

1) DDL (Data Definition Language): DDL is used by the database designer and programmers to specify the content and the structure of table. It is used to define the physical characteristics of record. It includes commands that manipulate the structure of object such as tables: For eg, to create table

Syntax:

CREATE TABLE table_name (field_name1 data_type1  field_name2 data_type2 ………);

CREATE TABLE Student (SN Number Fname text);

2) DML (Data Manipulation Language): DML is related with manipulation of records such as retrieval, sorting, display and deletion of records or data. It helps user to use query and display report of the table. It provide technique for processing the database. It includes commands like insert, delete, select, and update to manipulate the information stored in the database.

Syntax:

INSERT INTO table_name VALUES (list of values);

INSERT INTO student VALUES (1 RAM);

3) DCL (Data Control Language): All provides additional feature for security of table and database. It includes commands for controlling data and access to the database. Some of the example of this command are grant, commit, etc

Entity Relationship Database model (ER Model)

The entity relationship database model (ER diagram) is based on the perception of a real world that contains a collection of basic object called entities and relationship among these objects. The ER diagram is an overall logical structure of database that can be expressed graphically. It was developed to facilitates database design. The major objectives of ER diagram is to show relationship among different entities. It has following components.

1) Entity: The distinguishable object of this real world is known as entities. It has a set of properties which uniquely identifies an entity. For eg, if student is an entity then his/her name may be property. It is denoted by rectangle.

2) Attributes: Attributes are the properties possessed by an entity. They are represented by ellipse or oval sign. For eg, if student is an entity then its attribute can be registration number, name, roll no, class, address, etc.

3) Link: The flow of information is indicated by the link in ER diagram. It is simply denoted by a line. It is a connection of entity, attributes and relationships.

4) Relationships: A relationship is a association among several entities. It is represented by diamond. For eg, if teachers and students are two entities the association can be derived as teacher teachers students. It shows meaningful dependencies between several entities. There are 3 types of relationships. One to one. One to many, Many to many.

DBA (Database Administrator)

DBA is the most responsible person in an organization with sound knowledge of DBMS. He/she is the overall administrator of the program. He/she has the maximum amount of privileges for accessing database and defining the role of the employee which use the system. The main goal of DBA is to keep the database server up to date, secure and provide information to the user on demand.

Qualities of good DBA

  1. He/she should have sound and complete knowledge about DBMS and its operation.
  2. He/she should be familiar with several DBMS packages such as MS Access, MY SQL, Oracle etc
  3. He/she should have depth knowledge about the OS in which database server is running.
  4. He/she should have good understanding of network architecture.
  5. He/she should hove good database designing skill.

Responsibilities

  1. DBA has responsibility to install, monitor, and upgrade database server.
  2. He/she should has responsibility to maintain database security by creating backup for recovery.
  3. He/she has responsibility to conduct training on the uses of database.
  4. DBA defines user privilege, relationships and manages form, reports in database.

Normalization (v.imp)

The process of breaking down or decomposing as complex relation into simple relation. It reduces redundancy (unnecessary repetition of data) using principle of non-loss decomposition in which table are reduce to smaller tables without loss of information.

Normalization is the database design process in which complex database table is broken down into simple separate tables. It makes data model more flexible and easier to  maintain.

EF Codd has introduced few rules for normalizing the database in 1970 and these rules are known as normal forms. This process minimizes and controls the duplication of data in a database and also provides a rapid search for data from database.

Unnormalized database

Normalized database

Advantages of normalization

  1. It reduces data redundancy (duplication of data)
  2. It improves faster sorting and indexing.
  3. It simplifies the structure of the database table.
  4. It improves the performance of a system.
  5. It avoids loss of information.

Normal Forms

Let us consider a following unnormalized table.

A) 1NF ( First Normal form)

  1. 1NF sets the very basic rules for on organized database.
  2. It eliminates duplicate columns from the same table.
  3. It creates separate tables from each group of related data and identify each row with a unique column called primary key.

The objective of 1NF is to divide the base datas into logical units called tables.

In above table, we can see that column of subject nome and marks are repeated which are eliminated in 1NF.

B) 2NF (Second Normal form)

  1. It further addresses the concept of remaining duplicate data.
  2. It should be in first normal form.
  3. It removes the date that applies to multiple row of a table and place them in separate tables.

The objective of second NF is to take data i.e. partly dependent upon the primary key and enter the data into another table.

chapters.title: Economics : Meaning and Types
chapters.content:
Economics is the study of economic behaviors or economic activities of the people.

1. Consumption 2. Production 3. Distribution 4. Exchange 5. Public Finance.

Prof. Ragner Frisch has devided the term Economics into two parts in 1933 AD

1. Microeconomics microscopic view towards the economic agents that studies the smaller units of the economy eg a consumer, a producer, a product, etc

2 . Macroeconomics the economics that studies the larger or bigger economic phenomena eg poverty, unemployment , economic development, etc

Microeconomics vs. Macroeconomics  [ Differentiate between Microeconomics and Macroeconomics]

Mode of distinctionMicroeconomicsMacroeconomics
MeaningThe Term Microeconomics is derived from Greek word “Mikros” which literally means “small”.The Term Macroeconomics is derived from Greek word “Makros” which literally means “large”.
DefinitionMicroeconomics is one of the branches of economics which deals with individual or small economic issues such as a producer, a consumer, price of a product, individual demand, individual income, etc.Macroeconomics is one of the branches of economics which deals with aggregate or big economic issues such as poverty, unemployment, price level, national income, aggregate demand etc.
Known asIt is known as “price theory”.It is known as “income theory”
Assumptions: use of assumptionsThe laws and principles of Microeconomics are based on assumptions.The laws and principles are far from assumptions
EquilibriumMarket equilibrium is determined by market demand and supply in microeconomicsMarket equilibrium is determined by aggregate demand and aggregate supply.

Importance of Macroeconomics

1.Formulation of macroeconomic polices

2.Solving economic and social problems

3. Measurement of national income.

4. Maintaining economic and price stability.

Economy Based on the participation on international trade, the economy or economic situation of the countries in the world are divided into two parts. They are –

1. Closed Economy

2. Open Economy

Closed Economy : An economic system in which there is no provision of international trade is known closed economy. On the other words, a country is said to follow closed economic system in which the country trades within the country only. The country is self sufficient.

Open Economy : An economic system in which there is a provision of international trade is known open economy. On the other words, a country is said to follow open economic system in which the country trades between or among the countries. The cross boarder transaction takes between or among them. These countries are interdependent.

Closed Economy vs. Open Economy [ Differentiate between Closed economy and Open economy]

Mode of distinctionClosed EconomyOpen Economy
MeaningA closed economy is one in which the country trades only within its own boarders.An open economy is one in which the country trades with other nations as well.
DependencyThe countries with closed economy are entirely self-sufficient i.e. the country produces and distributes all the goods and services whatever is required to fulfill the demands and necessity of its people.The countries with open economy are dependent with each other in the world. They exchange the goods and services to fulfill the needs of the people of their countries
Import and ExportClosed economy prevents/restricts importing and exporting of the goods and services.Open economy allows importing and exporting of the goods and services.
InvestmentsBusiness sector invests within the nation only. Foreign investment is restricted in the domestic nationBusiness sector invests within and across the nation. Foreign investment is open .
Computation of GDPGDP = C+I+GGDP = C+I+G+ (X-M)

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Elasticity and its measurement
chapters.content:
Elasticity: It refers to the flexibility of something. It is the representative to change a particular thing due to its determining factors. Furthermore, elasticity can be defined as the proportionate (percentage) change in the quality of a thing due to a certain proportionate change in the determinants of the thing.

Elasticity of demand: A certain proportionate change in the quantity demand for a good due to a certain proportional change in the determinants of demand is known as elasticity of demand. It is denoted by Ed as given.

Ed = P r o p o r t i o n a t e c h a n g e i n q u a n t i t y d e m a n d e d P e r c e n t a g e c h a n g e i n d e t e r m i n a n t s d e m a n d

Demand: In general sense demand and desires are used as synonyms but in economic sense desire is just a wish to have a something but demand is an effective desire which is supported by willingness and ability to pay at any time factor and at any situation. Thus, the demand includes the following components

  1. Effective desire for goods and services
  2. Ability to pay
  3. Willingness to pay
  4. Per period of time

Law of Demand: The inverse relationship between quantity demanded and price other things remaining the same, is known as law of demand.

If P⇡ then Qd⇣ and if P⇣ then Qd⇡, other things remaining same.

Assumptions

  1. No change in price
  2. No change in taste
  3. No change in population
  4. No change in advertisement
  5. No change In season

Demand Schedule: The tabular presentation of various combination of price of a commodity and corresponding quantity demanded ot given period of time, other things remaining same. Eg is given below

Demand Curve: The graphical representation of demand schedule is called demand curve

Supply: The quantity of goods and services that the suppliers are willing and able to sell in the market at various price per period is called supply.

Law on supply: The law of supply explains direct relationship between price and quantity supplied of goods and services.

Assumptions

  1. No change in number on firms
  2. No change in technology
  3. No change in tax
  4. No change in price expectation
  5. No change in objective of firm

Supply schedule: A tabular representation of various combination of price and quantity supplied is called supply schedule.

Supply Curve: A diagrammatical representation of various units of price and quantity supplied schedule is called supply curve.

Elasticity on demand: The concept of elasticity of demand is a measure of degree of responsiveness of quantity demanded for a product to change in its determinants.

Elasticity of demand = % c h a n g e i n q u a n t i t y % c h a n g e i n d e t e r m i n a n t s

Types of Elasticity of Demand

  1. Price Elasticity of Demand
  2. Income Elasticity of Demand
  3. Cross Elasticity of Demand

1) Price Elasticity of Demand: It is defined as percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in its price. It is denoted as ‘Ep’ and given

Price Elasticity of demand (Ep) = P r o p o r t i o n a t e c h a n g e i n q u a n t i t y d e m a n d f o r p r o d u c t P r o p o r t i o n a t e c h a n g e i n p r i c e o f p r o d u c t

Price Elasticity of demand (Ep) = C h a n g e i n q u a n t i t y o r i g i n a l q u a n t i t y x 100 C h a n g e i n p r i c e o r i g i n a l p r i c e x 100

Ep = ∆ Q Q x 100 ∆ P P x 100

Ep = ∆ Q Q x P ∆ P

Ep = ∆ Q ∆ P x P Q

Where, Ep  = Elasticity of price

∆ = Small change

P = Original price (P1)

∆ P = Change in price (P2-P1)

Q = Original quantity demanded (Q1)

∆ Q =  Change in quantity demanded (Q2-Q1)

Q) The price of ice-cream is Rs 50 per units and its quantity demanded is 10 units. As per increases to Rs 75, quantity demanded falls to 4 unit. Calculate the price elasticity of demand.

P = Rs 5O (P1)

Q = 10 units

∆ P = P2-P1 = 75-50 =25

∆ Q = Q2-Q1 = 4-10 = -6

Then, Ep = ∆ Q ∆ P x P Q

Ep = - 6 25 x 50 10 = - 6 5 = -1.2

Due to the 1% rise in price there is 1.2% fall in quantity.

Q) Calculate Ep

∆ P = P2-P1 = 80-100 = -20

∆ Q = Q2-Q1 = 15-10 = 5

We know, Ep = ∆ Q ∆ P x P Q

Ep = 5 - 20 x 100 10 = - 5 2 =-2.5

Due to 2% fall in price there is 2.5% rise in quantity demanded.

Types of Price Elasticity of Demand

There are 5 types of price elasticity of demand. They are briefly presented below:

1) Perfectly Elastic Demand (Ep = ∞ )

If a negligible or small change in price brings about a huge change in quantity demand, it is known as perfectly elastic demand (Ep = ∞ ). It is presented as follows:

In the figure DD’ is perfectly elastic demand curve. Due to a small change in price, there is huge change in quantity demand. It is an imaginary case.

2) Perfectly Inelastic Demond (EP = 0)

If the quantity demand for a product remains unchanged whatever the percentage change in price it is Known as perfectly inelastic demand (Ep = 0). It is presented as follows:

In the figure,  DD’ is perfectly inelastic demand curve. Whatever the price is either (OP or OP1 or OP2) the quantity demanded is same. It happens in the quantity demanded for acute necessities like “Salt”, “medicine” etc.

3) Unitary Elastic demand (Ep = 1)

If percentage change in quantity demanded is exactly equal to the percentage change in price, then the demand is known as unitary elastic. (% ∆ P = % ∆ Qd). It is presented as follow

In the figure DD’ is unitary elastic demand in which % ∆ P = % ∆ Qd is PP1 = QQ1. It is a rare case.

4) Relatively Elastic or more Elasticity demand (Ep > 1)

If a certain percentage change in price brings about more than that percentage change in quantity demanded for a product (% ∆ Q > % ∆ P)  .It is known as relatively elastic demand. It is presented as follows:

In the figure DD is the relatively elastic demand curve in which percentage change in quantity demand is greater than the change in price. This is observed in case of quantity demand for luxurious goods.

5) Relatively Inelastic (less elastic) demand

If a certain percentage change in price brings about less than that percentage change in quantity demanded for a product (% ∆ P > % ∆ Qd), it is known as relatively inelastic demand. It is presented as:

In the figure, DD is relatively less elastic or inelastic demand curve in which percentage change in price (15%) is greater than the percentage change in quantity demanded (5%). It is observed in case on the quantity demanded for basic necessities like price.

Q) What is price elasticity of demand? Explain its types.

Income Elasticity of Demond (Ey)

If a certain proportionate change in the level on income of the consumer brings about the certain proportionate change in the quantity demanded for a consumer for a product, it is known as income Elasticity of demand. It is denoted by (Ey) and given as:

Income Elasticity of demand = P r o p o r t i o n a t e c h a n g e i n d e m a n d P r o p o r t i o n a t e c h a n g e i n i n c o m e o f a c o n s u m e r

Ey = c h a n g e i n d e m a n d i n i t i a l q u a n t i t y d e m a n d c h a n g e i n i n c o m e i n i t i a l i n c o m e = ∆ Q Q ∆ y y

Ey = ∆ Q Q x y ∆ y = ∆ Q ∆ y x y Q

where, Ey = Income elasticity on demand

∆ = Small change

y = Original initial income (y1)

∆ y = Change in income (y2-y1)

Q = Original quantity demand

∆ Q = Change in quantity demanded (Q2-Q1)

Q) The income on Prerana is Rs 10,000 per months and her quantity demanded is 25 units of a good. As there is increases in her income to Rs 18,000 her demand for that product increases to 40 units calculate (Ey)

∆ y = y2-y1 = 18000-10000 = 8000

∆ Q = Q2-Q1 = 40-25 =15

Ey = ∆ Q ∆ y x y Q = 15 8000 x 10000 25

Ey = 0.75

It shows that quantity demanded increases by 0.75 due to 1% rise in income.

Types of Income Elasticity of demand

Broadly, there are three types or categories of income elasticity of demand. They are briefly presented as follows:

1. Positive income Elasticity of demand (Ey >0 )

If a certain percentage change in quantity demanded for a product is positive due to a certain percentage change in the income of the consumer is known as positive income elasticity of demand ie positive relationship between the level of income of a consumer and the quantity demanded for a product. It is presented as follows:

In the figure, DD is the positively sloped income demand curve. In which the quantity demanded has been increased OQ-OQ1. When the income of the consumer increases from OY-OY1. It has three categories.

a) Income elasticity of demand greater than 1 [Ey >1]

If a certain percentage change in income brings about more than that percentage change in the quantity demanded is known as income elasticity of demand greater than 1%.(% ∆ Q > % ∆ y)   It is presented as follows.

In the figure, DD is more elastic demand curve. In which (% ∆ Q > % ∆ y) . It happened in the quantity demanded of luxurious goods.

b) Income Elasticity of Demand less than 1 [Ey < 1]

If a quantity demanded of a consumer increases less than the percentage increment in the income or the consumer (% ∆ y > % ∆ Q). it is known as income elasticity of demand less than 1. It is presented as follows:

In the figure DD is the less elastic demand curve in which (% ∆ y > % ∆ Q). It happens in the quantity demanded of basic necessities.

c) Income Elasticity on Demand equal to 1 [Ey = 1]

If a certain percentage change in level of income result to the same percentage change in the quantity demanded of a consumer is known as income elasticity on demand. It is presented as follows.

In the figure DD is the unitary elasticity demand curve in which % ∆ Y = % ∆ Q It is a rare case.

2. Negative income Elasticity Demand [Ey < 0]

If a certain percentage change in income brings about a certain percentage change in the quantity demanded of a consumer for a product, it is known as negative income elasticity of demand. It is presented as follows:

In the figure DD is negatively sloped income demand curve. It shows as the income increases from OY to OY1 the quantity demanded decreases for OQ to OQ1 It happens in case of inferior goods.

3. Zero Income Elasticity of demand [Ey = 0]

If a certain proportionate change in income do not respond to quantity demanded for a good i.e. quantity demanded remains unchanged irrespective of the change in level of income, it is known as zero income elasticity of demand. It is presented as follows:

In the fig DD is the zero income elastic curve in which whatever the percentage change in income OY to OY1 to OY2, the quantity demanded is same at OQ level. It happens in the quantity demanded for salt, medicine etc.

Cross elasticity of Demand

If the proportionate change in quantity demanded of goods to the proportionate change in the price of a related goods i.e. substitute good or complementary goods is called cross elasticity of demand. Cross elasticity of demand is symbolized by ‘Exy’ and written as:

Exy = P e r c e n t a g e c h a n g e i n q u a n t i t y d e m a n d o f g o o d X P e r c e n t a g e c h a n g e i n p r i c e o f g o o d Y

Exy = ∆ Q x Q x x 100 % ∆ P y P y x 100 % = ∆ Q x ∆ P y x P y Q x

Where,

Exy = Cross elasticity demand between X and Y

∆ = Small change

Qx = Quantity demand of goods

Py = Price of X goods

Types or cross Elasticity on Demand

Since two goods are related in two different ways, there are two types of cross elasticity of demand. They are

a) Positive cross Elasticity (Exy > 0)

Positive cross elasticity of demand is only applied in the case of substitute goods like coffee and tea. It increases in price of another substitute goods and vice versa then it is called positive cross demand. Hence, increases in the price of commodity result to the rise in a quantity demand of a substitute good. It is presented as follows:

In the given fig: quantity demand of coffee is measured along OX-axis and price of tea measured a long OY-axis. When the price of tea increases from OP-OP1, the quantity demand for coffee also increases from OQ-OQ1. Hence the DD1 is the positive cross demand curve slopping upward to the right.

b) Negative cross elasticity (Exy < 0)

Negative cross elasticity of demand only applied in case of complementary goods like petrol and bus. If the quantity demanded for a goods increases with the decrease in price of other complementary goods and vice-versa, there it is called negative cross elasticity of demand. Hence the rise in the price of commodity results to decreases in quantity demands of complementary goods. It is presented below:

In the given figure, quantity demand of pen is measured along OX and price of ink is measured along 0Y. When the price of ink increases from OP-OP1, the quantity demand of pen decreases from OQ-OQ1. Hence DD1 is the negative cross elasticity demand curve sloping downward to the right.

Measurement of Price Elasticity of demand

  1. Total Outlay (Total Expenditure Method)
  2. Point Method

1. Total Outlay Method

The concept of measuring the price elasticity of demand by total outlay or total expenditure method was presented by Professor Alfed Marshall in his book principle of economy. He has explain the relationship between the price of a commodity and the total expenditure. Looking at the total expenditure pattern made by a consumer, it is decided that which economic class the consumer belongs to. It is studied under the following three headings.

a. Price Elasticity of demand greater than unity Ep > 1

If the total expenditure of the consumer increases with the following price, it is known as price elasticity of demand greater than unity.

b. Price Elasticity of demand equal to unity Ep = 1

If the total expenditure remains same whatever is the price, it is known as price elasticity of demand equal to unity.

c. Price Elasticity of demand less than unity Ep < 1

If the total expenditure falls along with fall in price and vice-versa, is known as price elasticity of demand less than unity. Ep < 1. It is presented with the help of following table:

In the table, in category ‘A’ as the price decrease from Rs 60-50. The total expenditure increases from Rs 60- Rs 100. It is Ep > 1.

In category B whatever is the price either Rs 40 or 30, the total expenditure is constant at Rs 120. It is Ep = 1

In category C as the price decreases from Rs 20 - 10, the total expenditure also decreases from Rs 100 Rs 60. It is Ep < 1.

It can be presented graphically as follows:

Measurement of this Elasticity Demand total Outlay Method

In the figure, ‘ab’ portion show that there is inverse relationship between the price and the total expenditure. It is Ep>1. As the price declines from OP1-OP2, the total expenditure increases from OTE1-OTE2 and vice versa. This type of expenditure pattern is observed made by the low income level people in the society.

The ‘bc’ portion shows that there’s a constant relation between the price and the total expenditure. It is Ep=1. As the price decreases from OP2-OP3 the total expenditure remains constant at OTE2. This type of constant relation is observed made by the constant income people or fixed salary persons in the society.

The ‘cd’ portion shows that there is a positive relation ship between price and total expenditure. It is Ep<1. As the price decrease from OP3-OP4, the total expenditure decrease from OTE2-OTE1. It is observed made by the higher income people in the society.

This is how measuring the price elasticity of demand by total outlay method helps to identify the economic status of people in the society looking at their expenditure pattern.

Q) What is price elasticity of demand ? How it is measured by total outlay or total expenditure method? [2+8=10]

2) Point Method

The point method of measuring the price elasticity of demand is the geometrical method which elasticity of price elasticity at different point of demand curve. In a straight (linear) demand curves, price elasticity of demand at a point is the ratio of the distance between the point of x-axis to the y-axis on the demand curve. It is presented as:

Ep = L o w e r s e g m e n t o f t h e d e m a n d c u r v e u p p e r s e g m e n t o f d e m a n d c u r v e

It is present with the help of following diagram

we have Ep = ∆ Q ∆ P x P Q = l o w e r s e g m e n t u p p e r s e g m e n t

Ep = Q Q 1 P P 1 x O P O Q

The price elasticity of demand at different point of the linear demand curve is presented as follows:

let us suppose ‘M’ is the midpoint. The price elasticity of demand at different parts of linear demand curve. ‘AB’ is given as below:

Price elasticity on demand = L o w e r s e g m e n t o f d e m a n d c u r v e U p p e r s e g m e n t o f d e m a n d c u r v e

i) At ‘M’ Ep = M B M A =1 [ because M is midpoint]

Ep = 1 at ‘M’ price elasticity of demand is unitary elastic

ii) At ‘D’ Ep = D B D A <1

Ep<1, price elasticity is relatively inelastic.

iii) At ‘B’ Ep = 0 A B = 0

Ep = 0, price elasticity is perfectly inelastic.

iv) At ‘C’ Ep = C B C A > 1

Ep >1, price elasticity is relatively elastic

v) At ‘A’ Ep = B A 0 = ∞

Ep = ∞ , price elasticity is perfectly elastic

Determinants of (Price) Elasticity on Demand

The elasticity of demand varies from goods to goods, time to time place to place and person to person. These responsible factors are known as determinants of demand.

Among the various determinants some ore explained below:

1) Availability of close substitutes: Goods with close substitutes tend to have more elastic demand than less or no substitutes because it is easier for consumers to switch from that good to others. Eg: Pepsi and Coca-cola

2) Luxuries VS necessities: The demand for necessary goods tends to be inelastic, Whereas the demand for luxury tends to be elastic. Salt, bread and electricity are generally regarded as necessities, we cannot live without them.

3) Time period: Goods tend to have less elasticity in the short-run rather than in the long run, because the consumer will have choice in the long term.

4) Level of income: It is a real fact that rich people do not respond to small change in price of goods and services. So, for rich people demand remain relatively inelastic.

5) Habitual goods: Wine, cigarettes etc are some example of habitual goods.  Demand for such habitual goods remains relatively inelastic to a change in price.

Elasticity of supply

The quantity of goods and services that the suppliers are willing and able to sale in market at various prices, per period of time is called supply. The certain percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price is called PES.

PES = % c h a n g e i n q u a n t i t y s u p p l y % c h a n g e i n p r i c e

or, PES = ∆ Q s ∆ p x P Q s

Qs = original quantity supplied, ∆ = change, P = Original price

P1=100, P2= 200, Q1= 50, Q2=80

∆ Qs = Q2-Q1 = 80-50 =30

∆ P = P2-P1 =200-100 =100

PES = ∆ Q s ∆ p x P Q s = 30 100 x 100 50

PES = 0.6 Shows that quantity supplied increases by 0.6% due to 1% rise in price

Types of Price Elasticity or supply

There are 5 types. Some of them are explained below:

1) Perfectly Elastic supply PES = ∞

If a very small change in price of a good brings huge change in quantity supplied is called perfectly elastic supply.

In the figure SS1 is a price elasticity of supply due to small change in price brings huge change in quantity supply.

2) Perfectly inelastic supply PES = 0

If the quantity supplied of a quantity remains unchanged due to huge change in price

As there is rise or fall in price it doesn't bring any changes in quantity supplied of a product.

3) Relatively elastic supply

If a certain percentage change in price brings huge change in quantity supplied of a product is called relatively elastic supply.

In the figure supply curve is denoted by SS1. In the beginning when the price of a product is P1, the corresponding quantity supplied is denoted by Q1. As there is increase in price of that product from P1 to P2 quantity supplied increases from Q1-Q2. Here, the percentage change in quantity supplied is greater than the percentage change in price. It shows supply more price elastic.

4) Relatively Inelastic Supply

If a certain percentage change in price brings about less than that percentage change in quantity supplied is called relatively inelastic supply.

The supply curve is denoted by SS1. In the beginning, when the price of a product is P1, the corresponding quantity supplied is denoted by Q1. As there is increase in price of that product from P1 to P2, quantity supplied increases from Q1-Q2. Here, the percentage change in quantity supplied is smaller than the percentage change in price. It shows that supply is inelastic or less price elastic.

5) Unitary Elastic supply (PES = 1)

If the percentage change in price and percentage change in quantity supplied are exactly equal, it is called unitary elastic supply.

Quantity supplied is measured on the horizontal axis (x-axis) and price is measured on the vertical axis (y-axis). The curve denoted by SS1 is the supply curve.

Here, the percentage change in price and quantity supplied are equal i.e. % ∆ Qs = % ∆ P). So, it is the case of unitary elastic supply.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Theory of production
chapters.content:
Production: Production refers to the transformation of inputs into the output. It can also be defined as the creation of utility in goods or adding value on goods and services. Seed to plant to grain to human resource, stone to statue etc

Production function: Production function is the physical or technical or engineering relationship between inputs and outputs it is presented as

Q = F (L, La, K, O, R, T, F, E, Tr…. ) where,

Q = Output

La = land

F = function or output

L= Labour

T = Technology

K = Capital

O = Organization entrepreneurial skills

E = Energy

Tr = Transportation change

Factors of Production

  1. Fixed Factors of Production
  2. Variable Factors of Production

Based on the time, period, there are two types of production function. They are:

  1. Short - Run (S-R) Production function
  2. Long - Run (L-R) Production function

1) Short Run Production Function [Q= F (L, K )]

It is the production function of short period of time in which some of the factors include can be change and some of the factors include cannot be change. It is denoted by Q= F (L, K ). We study law of variable proportion under it.

2) Long Run Production function [Q= F(L, K)]

It is the production function of long period of time in which every factor includes become variable factor inputs due to sufficiency of time to manage them. It is denoted by Q= F(L, K). We study, law of returns to scale under it.

Q) Differences between production functions.

1) Total Product (TP): The sum total of the output made by the employment of certain factor inputs at a given time is known os total product. It is denoted by ‘TP’ and given by

TP = ∑ MP i = MP 1 +MP 2 +MP 3 +………..+MP n

Where, TP = Total product

MP = Marginal product

i = 1, 2, 3 ….. n

2) Marginal product (MP): The additional output due to employment or use of one additional factor input is known as marginal product. It is also defined as the change in total product due to the use of one extra factor input. It is defined by ‘MP’ and given as

MP = ∆ T P ∆ N = ∆ T P 1 = ∆ TP = TP n = TP n-1

3) Average Product: Average product is the per unit output. It is denoted by ‘AP’ and obtained by dividing TP by number of factor input(s) employed (N)

AP = T P N

Law of Variable Proportion

The law of variable proportion the short-term (run) production function. What happens to the total output, if some of the factor inputs are kept constant and the variable factor inputs are continuously added up is studied under it. It is presented by Alfed Marshall looking at the agricultural data initially.

According to Alfed Marshall, “An increase in the capital and labour applied in the cultivation of land causes in general a less than the proportionate increase in the amount of the product raise unless it happens to coincide with an improvement in an art of agriculture.

Assumptions

  1. At least one factor of production should be fixed so that while adding the variable factors, the ratio between variable and fixed factor should be varies.
  2. Inputs are used in varying proportion.
  3. The technologies constant.
  4. Variable inputs are homogeneous in terms of quality and productivity.
  5. Short run production.

It is presented with the following hypothetical table.

In the table, till the employment of 3rd unit or labour, the TP increases at the diminishing rate after the 6th unit.

TP is maximum (90) units and beyond that level of employment, TP starts to decline.

AP and MP increases first starting from same level of output (10) units, they are equal at a 4th unit of labour employed (20) units and finally they decline.

The law of variable proportion is presented with the help of above figure:

I Stage:

  1. TP increases at the increasing rate
  2. MP increases faster than AP, reaches at its maximum point and start to decline.
  3. AP increases slower than MP and reaches to maximum point at the end of 1st stage in which AP=MP.

II Stage:

  1. TP increases at the diminishing rate and TP goes on increases unless the MP is positive.
  2. TP reaches at its maximum point when MP=0
  3. AP starts to decrease.
  4. MP continuously falls and MP=0 at the end of 2nd stage in which TP is maximum.

III Stage:

  1. TP declines due to negative MP (- MP)
  2. AP continuously falls but it doesn't become zero and negative.

Stage of production

A rational producer doesn't stop his/her production in the first stage because every additional labour force gives the increasing return. S/he doesn't choose the third stage also because the producer will be in double side negative advantage in it. In one hand, the total output decreases resulting to the fall in revenue, on the other the wages is to be paid to the labourer. Therefore, it is obvious that a rational producer always chooses the second stage for the continuity of the production in which ‘AP’ and ‘MP’ are positive.

Law of Return to Scales

It is the long run production function in which every factor inputs become the variable factors due to the sufficiency of time to manage or change them. What happens to the total output if we go on adding the every factors input simultaneously is studied under it. It is denoted as, Q = F (L, K). During the long run, the following three situations are observed.

1) Increasing Returns to sale (IRS)

If the total output increases more than the ratio of factor inputs employed, it is known as increasing return to sale. It is presented as follows:

Increasing returns the sale schedule.

In the table, as the labour and capital are doubled and tripled, the total output has increased more than double and triple respectively and has become 200 and 5OO units.

In the figure, 0a

  1. Economics
  2. Highly qualitative raw materials
  3. Excess capacity of few factors
  4. Highly efficient
  5. Managerial efficiency

2) Constant Return to scale (CRS)

If the total output increases as the ratio factors inputs employed, it is known as constant return to scale. It is presented as follows:

Constant return to scale

In the table, as the labour and capital are doubled and tripled the total output has increased exactly double and tripled respectively and has become 100 - 150 units.

In the figure 0a=ab=bc, it represents that total output has been increased as the ratio of factors inputs employed. It happens during long run due to

  1. Economics of scale
  2. Qualitative raw materials
  3. Proper ratio of fixed and factors in S-R
  4. Efficient
  5. Managerial efficiency

3) Decreasing Return to Scale (DRS)

If the total output increases less than the ratio factors inputs employed it is known as decreasing return to scale. It is presented as follows:

Decreasing Return to scale

In the table, as the labour and capital are doubled and tripled, the total output has increased less than doubled and tripled respectively and has become 90 and 120 units.

In the figure, 0a>ab>bc, it represents that total output has been increased less than the ratio of factor input employed. It happens only during

  1. Diseconomies of scale
  2. Use on comparatively low quality raw materials
  3. Improper ratio of fixed and variable factor in SR.
  4. Inefficient productive labour price.
  5. Managerial inefficiency etc.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Theory of consumer's behaviour
chapters.content:
Meaning and definition of utility

Utility can be defined as the quantity or ability or capability of a good or service interact within it that satisfies the human wants .

According to I.S. Nicholson, “Utility may be the quality, which makes a thing desirable."

According to Prof. Hibdon, “Utility is the ability of a commodity to satisfy a want.”

There're two approaches of utility. They are:

1) Cardinal utility approach: It was developed by new classicals like H.H. Gosen Stamely Jevons, Alfred Marshall, AJ Dupit etc According to them (this approach) the satisfaction or utility provided by the consumption of goods and services can exactly be measured quantitatively. They had developed measuring unit ‘Util’ to measure the satisfaction be studied the law on diminishing marginal Utility. The law of substitution, Theory of consumers surplus etc under it.

2) Ordinal utility Approach: It was developed and explained by JR Hicks, Slutsky, RGR Allen, Walrus, Vilfred Pareto etc. According to them, the utility cannot be expressed in terms of numbers as it is a psychological phenomena which differs from person to person, it can only be rank that the satisfaction provided by consumption is more or less. We study Indifference Curve Analysis (ICA), Hicks weak logical ordinary theory etc under it.

Q) Differences between Cardinal Approach and Ordinal Approach

Concept of Total Utility (TU), Marginal Utility (MU) and Average Utility (AU)

1) Total Utility (TU)

Total utility is the sum total of the individual satisfaction received by a consumers while consuming a bundle of goods. It is denoted by ’TU’ and given as

TU = ∑ MU i = MU 1 + MU 2 +MU 3 + …… + MU n

Where, MU = Marginal Utility, i = 1, 2, 3 . . . . n

2) Marginal Utility (MU)

Marginal utility is an individual utility received by consumer while consuming a bundle of goods. It can be defined as the change in total utility due to the consumption of one additional unit of the good. It is denoted by ‘MU’ and goes as

MU = ∆ T U ∆ Q = TU n - TU n-1

where, TU= Total Utility, Q = Units commodity consumed

3) Average Utility (AU)

Average utility is the per unit utility which, is obtained by dividing total utility by the units of commodity consumed. It is denoted by ‘AU’ and given as:

AU = T U Q , where TU = Total Utility, Q = Units of commodity consumed.

Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility

Introduction: The law of diminishing marginal utility was first introduced by German economist Herman Herrich (HH) Gossen in 1854 AD. It is known as Gossens first law. Later on, Prof. Alfred Marshall had explained and popularized through the book ‘Principles of Economics” 1890 AD. It is the one commodity model of utility analysis.

Statement: The law on diminishing marginal utility states that the marginal utility received by a consumer while consuming a bundle of goods goes on diminishing.

Definition: According to Alfred Marshall “The additional benefit which a person derives from a given increase of his stock or anything diminishes with every increase in stock that he already has.

Assumption: The law on diminishing MU is based on following assumptions

1) The consumer should be a rational person. S/he could try to maximize his/her utility by using his/her scarce resources.

2) Cardinal measurement of utility. The utility received by the consumption be measured or expressed quantitatively in terms of ‘util’.

3) Constant marginal utility of money. The marginal utility of money does not change over the consumption and it is same to all.

4) There is no time gap in the successive consumption.

5) Homogenous units on goods. The various units on good are identical/same in terms of shape, size, quantity, color, price etc

6) The taste and preference of the consumer should remains same declines the consumption.

Explanation: The law of diminishing marginal utility is presented with the help on following hypothetical table

Marginal utility schedule

When the consumers, consumes the units of goods. S/he receives lesser utilities in the successive consumptions as 20 utils in the first, 16 utils in 2nd, 12 utils in 3rd and so on. On the 6th unit on consumption, the consumer receives 0 Marginal utility in which S/he would receive highest satisfaction in total. Beyond that level of consumption the consumer receives disutility (-4 utils in 7th units). If he continues the consumption. It can be presented graphically as follows:

In the figure, MU is negatively sloped marginal utility curve that shows the inverse relationship between units on commodity consume and the marginal is received by the consumption. As, units of commodity consume, goes on increasing, the marginal utility goes on diminishing. Therefore, on the successive consumption the utility is received by the consumer goes on declining.

Limitations of the law

The law of diminishing marginal utility isn’t applied in the following cases.

1) Rare and curio goods: In case of the old stamp collection, old paper notes, coin collection or elephants, rhino horn or the tiger jaw collection This theory isn’t applied. Similarly in the collection of decorative items, this law isn’t applied because the collection of additional unit gives the higher satisfaction.

2) Habitual Goods: In the consumption on habitual goods like tobacco and tobacco goods, alcohol, drugs etc this theory isn’t applied i.e. the additional consumption gives the higher satisfaction to the consumer.

3) Goods of Entertainment: In case of watching TV serial or game shows or trick shows etc, the successive show gives the higher satisfaction

4) Unequal size and quality: If the consumer, consumes the goods of unequal size and of different quality, the successive consumption, make it the higher satisfaction

5) Not applicable incase of irrational consumer. If the consumer is irrational one, the additional unit provides the higher satisfaction to the consumer.

6) The cardinality of utility: In fact, the utility is entrustective phenomena it differs from time to time and person to person. Therefore, it can’t be measure exactly length, weight, time etc.

7) The marginal utility of money isn’t constant: This theory has assumed that the (MU) is constant, but in the reality the additional unit value of additional unit of money differs from person-to- person. Then, it's not a constant.

8) Measurement of utility of durable goods. The utility provided by the durable goods like television, cupboard, watch etc cannot be measured. Similarly, the utility provided by the anniversary or birthday cake revenge marriage cannot be imagine.

Nature of TU, AU and MU

The nature of TU, AU and MU is presented with the help on following table and diagram.

Total, Average, Marginal utilities

Nature of TU

  1. TU increases from the beginning.
  2. TU increases at the diminishing rate.
  3. TU reaches at any level.
  4. Finally TU declines.

Nature AU

  1. AU decreases from the beginning.
  2. AU decreases slower than MU.
  3. AU never reaches to zero neither it becomes negative.

Nature of MU

  1. MU decreases from the beginning.
  2. MU decreases faster than AU.
  3. It becomes zero and negative too.

Relationship between TU, AU and MU.

  1. TU increases at the rate of MU i.e. MU is rate of change in TU.
  2. TU increase as long as MU
  3. TU is maximum when MU is zero.
  4. TU starts to decline when MU becomes negative.
  5. AU and MU Start to decline from the same point.
  6. AU and MU both decrease but MU decreases faster than AU so that MU becomes zero and negative but AU doesn’t.

Law of substitution

The law or substitution was first presented by German economist H.H. Gossen in 1854 AD. It is known as Gossen's second law. It was developed and popularized by Alfed Marshall in his book “Principles of Economics” in 1890 AD. It is a two commodity model of utility analysis.

The law on substitution states that in order to maximize the utility, the consumer allocates his budget in two goods. TO get the maximum satisfaction the consumer substitute the units of lesser utility by the units of higher utility. S/he continues this unless and until the marginal utilities received from the last unit of both goods are equal which is equal to the marginal utility of human. Therefore be law on substitution is also known as law of equal marginal utility.

According to Alfred MarShall, “In order to maximize the utility, the consumer allocates his income in such a way that the ratio of marginal utility to price of each goods be equal to marginal utility of money.”

Assumptions:

  1. The law of substitution is based upon the following assumptions.
  2. Consumer should be a rational person.
  3. Cardinal measurement of utility.
  4. Applicability on diminishing marginal utility.
  5. Utilities derived from various goods are independent.
  6. Money income of the consumer is given and fixed.
  7. Prices of the goods are given.
  8. Constant MU of money

Explanation

Let us suppose, consumer has Rs 50 and s/he consumes two good 'x' and ‘y’ which costs Rs 10 each so that the consumer can consume any five units only of either of goods or both of them. It is presented with the help of following hypothetical table.

TU(x+y) = 20+16+12+15+12 = 75

In the table, if the consumer allocates his full resource to consume the ‘x’ good only s/he receives 60 utils at the total satisfaction (20+16 +12+15+12 = 75). On the other hand if the consumer allocates his budgets to consume ‘Y’ good only s/he receives 45 utils at the total utility (15+12+9+6+8 = 45). In order to maximize the utility, the consumer consumes by mixing the units of the good rather consuming the units of only one good. For that the consumer substitute the units of lesser utility (5th unit of ‘x’ good) by the unit of higher utility (1st unit of ‘y’ good). This process continues until the MU receives from the last unit of both goods are equal. Here, if the consumer consumes 3 units of ‘x’ goods and two units of ‘y’ goods. S/he receives the highest utility as 75 utils [TU(x+y) = 20+16+12+15+12 = 75] which no other combination gives. This can be presented graphically as follows:

In the figure, the consumer gets maximum satisfaction when the marginal utilities received from ‘x’ good and ‘y’ good are different i.e. which is equal to ab = cd which is equal to the marginal utility of money. It is the best possible combination in which the consumer maximizes his/her total.

While adding up one more unit of ‘y’ good the consumer gains the utility equal to the shaded part in the figure 'cdhg’. For that s/he needs to sacrifices one unit of ‘x’ good equal to the shaded part in the figure ‘abfe’. Here, ‘abfe' > ‘cdhg’ i.e. loss > gain. Therefore, the total unity should not be maximum.

Hence, in order to maximize the utility, the marginal utilities receives from the consumption of last units of both good should be equal.

Criticisms or limitations

The limitations of law of equi-marginal utility are as follows

i) Utility cannot be measured in cardinal number. It is a psychological phenomena that differs from people-to-people and time to time. Therefore, it cannot be presented exactly interims of number.

ii) Diminishing marginal utility isn’t applied. There are so many exceptional cases on the law on diminishing marginal utility due to which there would be problem to applied the law of Substitution.

iii) Marginal utility of money isn’t constant. The MU of money differs from people to people and time to time.

iv) Utilities are dependent: This theory has assumed that the utility are independent but in reality they are inter dependent.

v) Rational consumer is rare: This theory is based upon the rational consumer that allocates the budget maximize the total utility but in reality people consume the good without counting the utilities.

Despite of these limitations the consumer maximize the satisfaction while s/he consume the goods by mixing the various units of two or more than two goods.

Law of consumer’s Surplus

The concept on consumer's surplus was first introduced by French engineer as well as economist Arsene Jules (AJ) Dupit in social benefit. Later of Alfred Marshall introduced it in the utility analysis i.e. in consumption. Consumer surplus is defined as the willingness to pay (or anticipated price or expected price or estimated price) and the actual price amount i.e.

consumer's surplus = Willingness to pay - Actual price

let us Suppose, a consumer is ready to pay willing to pay Rs 7500 for a watch. If she finds it in Rs 7100 in the market, the consumer's surplus is Rs 400 (7500-7100)

According to Alfred Marshall. “Excess of the price which a consumer would be willing to pay rather than go without a thing over that which he actually does pay is the economic measure of this surplus satisfaction. It may be called consumer surplus.”

The theory of consumer's surplus is based upon the following assumptions:

  1. Expected price should be more than actual price.
  2. MU must be greater or equal to price of commodity.
  3. Utility can be measured in cardinal number i.e. utils.
  4. Consumer is a rational person.
  5. Constant marginal utility of money.

It is presented with the help of hypothetical table:

In the table, the consumer is ready to pay Rs 140 because of the total utility that s/he receives from the consumption of 4 units of goods. But s/he actually pays Rs 80. Then, the consumer's surplus is the net difference between willingness to pay and actual paid amount. i.e.

140-80 = 60 = 30+20+10+0

It is presented graphically as follows:

In above figure, consumers are willing to make payment equal to the area of ‘BQ’ to purchase the ‘OQ’ amount or goods. The maximum willingness to pay price Pw is ‘BA’. But actually the market price is only 'OP’. As the willingness to pay price is higher than the price that the consumer has to pay, there is consumer surplus. Consumer surplus is equal shaded area of triangle PwAB. Thus, in graphical terms, area below the demand curve but about the price line is equal to the consumer surplus.

Criticisms of consumer's surplus

This law of consumer surplus is criticized by the several economists including Nicholas Kardor, JK Hicks and P B Samuelson on several grounds.

1) Marginal utility of money is not constant. This law assumes that the marginal utility of money remains constant. But in practical life, when quantity of money increases, MU of money decreases.

2) Actual Price may be greater than expected price. The theory of consumer surplus assume that expectful price is greater than the actual price.

3) Utility is not measurable: This law of consumer surplus is based on the assumption that utility can be measured quantitatively in the term of money, but quality is a subjective phenomena, it cannot be measured quantitatively.

4) It is not applicable to necessary goods. It is not applicable in necessary and luxurious goods. A consumer is simply willing to acquire goods.

5) The title is wrong: The title of this theory is consumer's surplus. But the actual title should be buyer's surplus.

6) It neglects complementary and substitute goods: The utility of any commodity depend on other commodity, but this theory does not explain the role of complementary goods and substitution goods.

Importance of consumer surplus

The concept of consumer surplus has the following significance.

1) To determine prices of goods and services: This is very useful to determine prices of goods and services. If the consumer surplus is very high, the producer can raise the price of goods and services and vice-versa.

2) To determine the tax rate: The law of consumer surplus is useful to government to determine tax rate. The government can determine high rate tax on goods and services that have more consumer surplus and vice-versa.

3) Guidelines for consumer and producer: The law of consumer's surplus can be a guideline for both consumer and producer. It can helps the consumer to maximize the surplus.

4) Cost benefit Analysis: The law of consumer surplus helps in cost benefit analysis as well as in project selection if the expected cost incurred is less and benefit is more, the project may be selected.

5) International trade: The law of consumer's surplus is significant to estimate the gain from the international trade. The government can produce and trade those types of goods and services in international market which have more consumer's surplus.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Revenue and cost curves
chapters.content:
Market: It is a place where by trading of good and services takes place. It is a mechanism where by selling and buying of goods and services takes place.

Market Structures

  1. Perfect competition market
  2. Imperfect competition market
  3. Monopoly market
  4. Monopolistic
  5. Duopoly
  6. Duopolistic
  7. Oligopoly
  8. Oligopolistic

Perfect competition market

It is in which there are large numbers of buyers and sellers trading the homogeneous goods. There is the availability of close substitute goods and entry and exist free in this market. Industry determines the price (price maker) and each business firm is the price taker or price receiver due to which the price of a product is constant in this market. These is free mobility of factor of production and no to transportation change is applied in this market. There is perfect knowledge of market to both buyers and sellers. Government doesn't play the active role in production of goods and services. i.e. government plays the role or guardianship only.

Monopoly Market

Monopoly market is one of the imperfect competition market structures in which there are large numbers of buyers but a single seller of a product. The products are different and the entry and exit is difficult in this market. As the firm and industry is same. The firm itself is the ‘price taker’ and ‘price maker’ both. The monopoly is either run by government or protected by government. NOC, Salt trading corporation etc are the government run monopoly business in Nepal. In order to sell the additional unit, the monopolist is compelled to reduce the price. So, in private run monopoly, price is differentiated.

Q) Differences between Perfect Competition Market and Monopoly Market.

Concept of Total, Average & Marginal Revenue

Revenue: The receipt against the sale of goods and commodities known as service. It is denoted as ‘R’.

1) Total Revenue (TR): The sum on the receipt against the sale of production units of goods within a certain time is known as Total revenue. lt is denoted as ’TR” and given as:

TR = PxQ or  TR = MR 1 +MR 2 +MR 3 +MR 4 +………..+MR n

Where: P=Price, Q=Quantity Sold, MR=Marginal Revenue

2) Average Revenue (AR): It is defined as the per unit revenue and obtained by dividing TR by the units of quantity sold i.e. AR = T R Q = P x Q Q =P

3) Marginal Revenue (MR): It is the individual revenue. It can be defined as the change in total revenue due to the sale of one additional unit of the goods. It is defined as ‘MR’ and given as:

MR = ∆ T R ∆ Q = ∆ T R 1 = ∆ TR = TR n +………..+TR n-1

Concept of TR, AR and MR under Perfect Competiton on Market

Perfect Competition market is the market structure in which there are large buyers and sellers trading the homogenous goods. Industry determines the price and each business firm receives it. Therefore price is constant in the market. The concept of TR, AR and MR under it is presented with the help of following table and diagram.

TR, AR and MR schedule under Perfect Competition

TR, AR and MR curve under Perfect competition

In the table the price is constant at RS. 20. Therefore at each level of quantity sold the price is equal to MR and AR. In the fig, due to this reason price line, MR and AR curves overlap with each other which is parallel to x-axis.

In the table, the price is constant, TR increases at a constant rate of Rs 20 due to which TR becomes the rectangular bisector in the figure.

Relation between TR, AR and MR under perfect competition market

  1. Price AR & MR is same.
  2. Price AR and MR curve is same which is horizontal and parallel ‘x-axis’
  3. TR increases at the rate of MR so that it becomes the bisector of the rectangular axes.

Concept on TR, AR and MR under Monopoly

Market: Monopoly Market is one of the imperfect competition market structures in which there are large number of buyers and a seller for a product. The industry and firm is same under it. If itself determines the price of product and launch it. In order to sell, the additional units of the group, the monopolist gradually needs to reduce the price. The concept of TR, AR & MR under the monopoly market is presented with the help of table and diagram.

TR, AR and MR schedule under Monopoly Market.

In the table up to the 5th unit of sale MR is positive and TR increases at the rate of MR. In the figure, unless the MR is positive TR goes on increasing.

At the 6th unit of sell, MR is zero and TR is Rs 30 which is maximum in the fig. Similarly, beyond the 6th unit of sell, MR is negative (-2) due to which TR declines to Rs 28

In the table, price and AR is same which goes on decreasing on the successive sale of the units. In the fig, AR is the downward sloping curve which represents that on the addition sell the AR declines. It is also, the demand curve and price line.

Q) Derive TR, AR and MR under the monopoly market [10 MARKS]

Relation between TR, AR and MR under the monopoly market

  1. TR increases unless the MR is positive.
  2. When MR is 0, TR is maximum.
  3. When MR is -ve, TR starts to decline.
  4. MR and AR starts from same point, they decrease from the beginning but MR decreases faster than AR.
  5. MR becomes 0 and -ve but not AR on the continuous sell of unit or goods.

Cost: The payment to the owner of factor of production against its use in the production process. It is the rewards due to the contribution of factor of production in the production process of goods and services.

Short Run (S-R) Total Cost

1) Total Fixed cost (TFC): Fixed cost is the payment made to the fixed factors of production like land, building plant and machineries top level managers. The sum of there cost is known as TFC. It is applied before the production starts and remains same or constant or fixed analyzing the short run, whatever is the level of output.

2) Total Variable Cost (TVC): Variable cost is the payment to the variable factor inputs like raw materials, fuel energy, transportation, working level labourer etc. The sum of cost is known as the TVC. It is not applied in the production has not been started and varies along with variation in the level output.

3) Total Cost (TC): Short-run total cost is the sum on total fixed cost and total variable cost.

TC = TFC+TVC

Derivation of Total Cost Curves

The total cost curves are derived from the following hypothetical Total Cost Schedule:

In the table, the total fixed cost is same or constant or fixed at Rs 60 due to which the TFC curve, is parallel and horizontal to x-axis. It is applied even if the production doesn't start i.e. at 0 level of output and remains same irrespective with level of output.

The total variable cost (TVC) is applied only when the production starts. As the law of variable proportion is applied, the TVC increases fast for two short time, increases slowly and finally increases fast. Due to this reason, the TVC curve is in inverse ’S’ shape. The total cost is the sum of TFC and TVC i.e. TC = TFC+TVC. The nature of TC curves is as the nature of TC curves is as the nature of TVC curve.

Short Run Average Cost and Cost Curve

1) Average Fixed Cost (AFC): The average fixed cost is the per unit fixed cost which is obtained by dividing TFC by the level of output ‘Q’ i.e. AFC = AFC/Q. AS the, TFC is constant in the short run the AFC continuously decreases with the increase in level of output. Thus, the AFC Curve gives the shape Hyperbola. It is presented as follows:

2) Average Variable Cost (AVC): Average Variable  Cost is the per unit variable cost of production. It is calculated by dividing total variable cost (TVC) by the corresponding horizontal distance measuring the level of output. It produces a U-shape AVC curve and presented below:

3) Average Total Cost (ATC): Average Total Cost is per unit variable cost production which is obtained by dividing total cost by output i.e. AC=TC/Q. Graphically AC at each level of output is presented  by the distance on the vertical arts of divided by the corresponding horizontal of it.

4) Marginal Cost (MC): Marginal cost is the additional cost on total cost added by the production of one more unit of output.

MC n = TC n - TC n-1

Where, ’n’ is total units of output. In other words, MC is the change in total cost in response to the change in production.

Relationship between S-R Average cost (AFC, AC, AVC, MC)

The relationship between S-R average costs is presented into the help of following figure:

  1. The AFC is in the shape of hyperbola because the TFC is constant in S-R.
  2. AVC, AC and MC are in ‘U-shape’ because of the application of the law of variable proportion in S-R.
  3. Minimum point of MC comes easier than the minimum points of AVC and AC.
  4. When MC increases it passes through the minimum points or AVC and AC.
  5. Before the minimum points of AVC and AC, MC < AVC and MC < AC respectively
  6. The main points of AC lies at up-right of the main point of AVC because:

a) AC = AFC+AVC

b) After OQ 2 level of output, the falling rate of AFC > the rising rate of AVC, it pulls down the AC. [falling ‘ef’ rising ‘bd’]

c) After OQ 3 level of output, the rising rate of AVC > falling rate of AFC, it pushes ‘AC’ up.

d) At OQ 3 level of output, the falling rate of AFC = the rising rate of AVC, it helps to attain the minimum point to ‘AC’

chapters.title: Unit 1: Nature of Management
chapters.content:
Concept of Management:

Management is the activity of directing leading to achieve the predetermined goals. In other sense, the word management is combination of three word that is manage-men-t (tactfully) which means to manage human resources tactfully for mobilization of other physical resources to meet goal.

According to Robbins "management is the process of getting things done by other things with the aim of achieving goal effectively and efficiently.”

In conclusion, management is the process of PODSLC. PODSLC means planning, organizing, staffing, directing, leading and controlling respectively. It is an art of getting things done through people for the achievement of goals. Principle of management have been universally applied. It is essential for organizational effectiveness. Good management achieved the organizational objectives with the best use of all kind of resources.

Level of management:

The level of management are as follows:

1. Top level of management: Top level management consists of board for director (BOD). Chief executive officer (CEO), general manager and managing director. Top level management is the supreme body of an organization they are responsible in formulating long term plans, policies, mission, vision, goals, etc. of an organisation.

Important function of top level management:

Important function of top level management are as follows:

i. To determine the goals of an organization

ii. to make plan and policies to attain a goal.

iii. to set up an organization structure to conduct the operation is for plan

iv. To provide overall direction in the organization

v. Investing in research and development

2. Middle level of management: Middle level of management consists of head of department, branch manager, division head, section head etc. Middle level management are primarily responsible to implement the policies and plan developed by the top level management. Middle level management are essential to bridge the upper and lower level of organization.

Important function of middle level management:

The important function of middle level management are as follows:

i. To interpret the policies found by the top level management

ii. To recruit and select suitable operative supervisory staff.

iii. To assign duties and responsibilities for first line officer.

iv. To motivate personal (staff) to attend a productivity and reward them

properly

3. Lower level of management : Lower level management consists of foreman, supervisors, sales officer, marketing officer, etc. lower level management is also known as fast line management and operating level management. It is directly concerned with the direction and control of the performance of the operative non-managerial employees.

Important function of lower level management:

The important function of lower level management are as follows:

i. Instruction and guidance to the operating employees and workers.

ii. Preparation of short term plan.

iii. Assignment of duties: it assigns job, duties and responsibilities to the non-managerial employees.

iv. To arrange the necessary tools and equipment, materials etc. for the workers.

v. To solve the problems of workers

vi. To inform the unsolved problems of workers to the management.

Feature of Management:

The feature of management are as follows:

1. Process: management is a process. the function short is planning, organizing, directing, staffing, leading and controlling are included in the process which proper coordination of resources by means of managerial function.

2. Group Activity: management is based on group activities. The significance of management is the group participation both note industrialization. a group can easily and effectively attain the goals of organization rather than an individual.

3. Purposeful: every management activity is purposeful. Management it helps in or contributes greatly for efficient and effective use of different resources to achieve the goal. The main objective of management is to maximize the productivity through minimum sources.

4. Both science and art: management is both science and art. It is science because it is based on same basic principle of universal application. it is also in because the result of an organization depends upon the personal skills, efficiency and experience of manager and his subordinates.

5. Profession: management is also profession because it has the feature of profession like specific knowledge, formal education, service motive, ethical codes etc. So, in today's world measurement is Taken as a profession.

6. Universal: management is universal in nature. It is necessary and practice in almost all types of organization. Management institute query or essential where there is human activity. It means that wherever there is a human activity, there is management. The principle of management is universally applicable.

7. Dynamic: management is a continuous and dynamic activity. Principle of management and not rigid. The principles are flexible as for the need and requirement of time and organization. The system of management of today may not be suitable or applicable tomorrow. So, management modifies its style and system is for time and situation which saves the organization to adjust itself in changing environment of business.

8. Social Process: management is a social process because it consists of getting things done through others. This involves dealing with people. the effort of human beings has to be directed, coordinated and regulated by management.
