chapters.title: Chapter 12: Basic concept of organic chemistry
chapters.content:
Organic Chemistry: The branch of chemistry which deals with the study of structures, properties and chemical transformation(reactions) of organic compounds. Organics chemistry is the study of hydrocarbon and its derivative.

Organic compound: The compound that are made of carbon and hydrogen and their derivatives are organic compound. In organic compound, elements are covalently bonded with each other.

Difference between organic and inorganic compounds.

Isomer: Those compound that have same Molecular formula but different arrangement of atoms.

Catenation: Carbon forms covalent bond with other carbon atoms and forms a long chain which is known as catenation

Sources of Organic Compound

  1. Plants
  2. Animals
  3. Natural gas and petroleum
  4. Fermentation (Making curd from milk/alcohol)
  5. Coal
  6. Synthesis

Classification of Organic Compounds.

On the basis of structure organic compounds mainly classified into two groups.

A) Open chain Compounds (aliphatic Compound)

Organic compound in which carbons are linked together forming a chain is known as Open Chain Compound. These are also known as acyclic compound or aliphatic compound.

Open chain compounds are further classified into following groups:

Alkanes: Alkanes contain carbon to carbon single bond only. They are also known as saturated hydrocarbon and are also known as “Paraffins”

Alkenes: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbon in which at least one carbon to carbon double double bond is present in their molecule. Alkenes are also known as "Olefins”.

Alkynes: Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbon in which at least one carbon to carbon triple bond is present in their molecule. Alkynes are also known as “Acetylenes”.

B. Cyclic compound or closed chain compound

Cyclic compounds those in which terminal (end) carbon are linked together forming ring type structure and ring may be one or more. They are classified as:

a. Alicyclic compound: These are cyclic or closed chain compound but they resemble open chain compound in many aspect. Similar to that of aliphatic compound these are also further classifieds cycloalkanes, cycloalkanes and cycloalkanes, for eg,

b. Aromatic Compound: In this type of compound mainly hexagonal ring is present with alternate double bond (benzoid ring) and are very stable in nature than alicyclic compound. Aromatic compound are also Known as arenes.

Homocyclic and Heterocyclic compound:

Both homocyclic and heterocyclic compound can be classified as homocyclic and heterocyclic compound. If the cyclic ring is formed by carbon only then it is known as homocyclic compound. Example of homocyclic compound is benzene, cyclohexane. If ring is formed by carbon and other element then the compound is known as heterocyclic compound. The element involve ring formation is known as heteroelement. For eg,

Functional Groups And Alkyl Groups

Organic Compounds are composed of two parts, a reactive part known as functional group and skeleton part known as alkyl part or alkyl radical.

Thus, Functional group is defined as an atom of group of atoms which largely determines the chemical properties of the organic compound. The compound with same functional group react is as a similar manner even though they have different alkyl radical.

Functional group a different compounds and their classes.

Homologous series:

When the compound belonging to same class are arranged in order of increasing molecular weights, a set of compounds is formed in which each successive members differ by -CH 2 Unit, Such group organic compounds is known as homologous series. Individual members of homologous Series are called homologous and the phenomenon is known as homology.Examples.

Homologous series of alkanes (C n H 2n+2 )

CH 4 , H 3 C-CH 3 , H 3 C-CH 2 -CH 3 , H 3 C-CH 2 -CH 2 -CH 3 …………..

Homologous series of alcohols (C n H 2n+1 OH)

CH 3 -OH , H 3 C-CH 2 -OH , H 3 C-CH 2 -CH 2 -OH , H 3 C-CH 2 -CH 2 -CH 2 -OH…………..

Characteristics of Homologous series

  1. All members of Homologous series can be represented by same general formula.
  2. Two successive members of the series differ by -CH 2 unit in their molecular formula.
  3. The members of same homologous series have similar chemical properties.
  4. The members of same homologous series have same functional group.

Types of formula Used in Organic Chemistry.

a. Empirical formula

Empirical formula of compound is the simplest formula that shows the simplest whole number ratio of atoms present in one molecule of particular compound. For example, Glucose has 6 carbon atoms, 12 hydrogen atoms and 6 oxygen atoms and hence empirical formula is (H 2 O).

b. Molecular Fomula

Molecular formula shows the actual numbers of atoms a various elements present in molecules. For eg molecular formula of glucose is (C 6 H 12 O 6 ). It indicates that one mole of glucose contains 6 moles of C, 12 moles a H and 6 moles of O.

Molecular formula = [Empirical formula]xn

where, n = 1, 2, 3, 4, etc. OR, n = [ molecular formula weight / empirical formula weight ]

c. Structural formula

Structural formula shows how the various atoms are linked together in a molecule the structural formula also called as graphic formula.

d. Contracted formula (Condensed formula)

The structural formula of compound written in the condense form is called condensed or contracted formula. Eg,

Band Line Structural Formula

Band line structural formula is a shorthand way of writing organic structural formulas.

  1. The carbon atoms and the hydrogen atoms attached to them are not shown.
  2. Only the bonds between the Carbon atoms are shown as line.
  3. The vertices and end of lines represent the carbon atoms.
  4. Any unfilled valences on carbon are assumed to be filled by hydrogen atoms.
  5. All atoms other than carbon plus any hydrogen atoms attached to them are shown.

To be continue..

chapters.title: Part B - Ch6: Introduction to Biology
chapters.content:
The study of life and living things, both plants and animals is called biology.

  1. The term Biology was coined by Lamarck and Treviranus.
  2. Father of Zoology is Aristotle.
  3. Father of Botany is Theophrastus.
  4. Father of Biology is Aristotle.
  5. Father of medicine is Hippocrates.
  6. Father of concept of organic evolution is Empedocles.

Two main branches of biology.

  1. Botany
  2. Zoology

Branches of Biology

  1. Anatomy
  2. Morphology
  3. Histology
  4. Physiology
  5. Ecology
  6. Taxonomy
  7. Genetics
  8. Cytology

Name of the branches

  1. Morphology: Study of external features of organism Anatomy. Study of internal structures of organisms.
  2. Histology: Study of structure and function of tissues.
  3. Cytology: Study of structure and functions of cells and cell organelle.
  4. Genetics: Study of hereditary characters and their inheritance. Ecology: Study of relationship between living organisms and environment.
  5. Embryology: Study of formation and development of embryo upto  hatching on birth.
  6. Evolution: Study of origin of life and evolution to modern plants and animals.
  7. Physiology: Study of life processes in animals and plants.
  8. Taxonomy: Study of classifications of organisms and its principles.
  9. Pathology: Study of diseases caused by organisms.
  10. Paleontology: Study of plant or animal fossils.
  11. Microbiology: Study of micro-organism or microbes.
  12. Bio-chemistry: Study of chemistry of living organisms.
  13. Bio-technology. Technique of using organisms to modify the organisms and their products for human benefit.
  14. Limnology: Study of freshwater and their inhabitants.

Branches of Zoology

  1. Entomology
  2. Helminthology
  3. Ornithology
  4. Parasitology
  5. Herpetology
  6. Mammalogy
  7. Ichthyology

Name of the branches

  1. Protozoology: Study of unicellular organisms
  2. Para-zoology: Study of Porifera or sponges
  3. Cnidology: Study of coelenterates
  4. Helminthology: Study of helminth worms
  5. Parasitology: Study of parasitic worms
  6. Entomology. Study of insects
  7. Araeneology: Study of spiders
  8. Aphidology: Study of aphids

Relation of Biology with Other Sciences

Relation with Chemistry

  1. The genetic materials such as DNA and RNA are formed by the chemicals.
  2. The enzymes, hormones, etc secreted in animals are exclusively chemicals.

Relation with Physics

  1. Certain life processes such as movement of minerals etc are dependent on the physical phenomenon.
  2. Various physiological activities of plants are dependent on intensity of light as well as energy.

Relation with Sociology

  1. Animal behaviour and social relationship are dependent on the social activities.
  2. Due to social nature many animal follows the pattern of the social customs.

Relation with Geography

Distribution of animals and plants vary with different geographical factors such as temperature climate, topography, altitude etc.

Scope of zoology

  1. Field of Health and Disease
  2. Field of agriculture
  3. Field of Industry

Characteristics of Living Things

  1. Definite shape and size
  2. Cellular structure and protoplasm
  3. Movement and locomotion
  4. Nutrition
  5. Respiration
  6. Metabolism
  7. Excretion
  8. Irritating
  9. Reproduction
  10. Growth
  11. Life cycle
  12. Repair of injured part
  13. Ageing and death

Origin and Evolution of Life

Evolution : A slow and progressive change resulting into complexity from simple and lower organisms which has taken place during millions of years on earth is called evolution.

The plants, the animals, the planets, the stars and even the earths topography change continuos. The change in relation to plants and animals are described under organic evolution.

a. Special creation of Life

b. Spontaneous Generation of Life

c. Theory of Biogenesis

  1. Redis experiment
  2. Spallanzanis experiment
  3. Pasteur’s experiment

d. Cosmozoic Origin of Life / Interplanetary Theory

e. Theory of Castastrophism

f. Steady State Theory

a. Special creation of life: Theory was proposed by Spanish priest Father Saurez (1548-1671 AD). According to this view point earth and the different forms of life were created by a supernatural power of God.

b. Spontaneous Generation of life: According to this view, life could came from non-living things. Till the end of 17th century, scientists and philosophers believed that living things could arise spontaneously from non-living things. This concept was held by early Greek philosophers like Thales Anaximander, Plato etc

c. Theory of Biogenesis: The theory of biogenesis tells that origin of life took place from pre-existing life. Many scientists supported the theory of biogenesis through their experiments. The Lamarck experiments that established the theory of biogenesis were Redi’s experiment, Louis Pasteur’s experiment.

Redi’s Experiment

Italian Physician Franciso Redi (1621-1697) demonstrated that fly maggots weren’t created from meat. To proof this idea, Redi made an experiment using two jars. He kept lumps of boiled made in both jars. One jar was left an uncovered and other was covered with the gauze or muslim cloth and others with parchment paper.

Observation: After few days, Redi’s observed fly maggots only in the uncovered jars where flies could lay their eggs on meat.

Conclusion: On the basis of the above observation, it could be stated that the fly maggots were originated not from inanimate substances but from their pre-existing forms present in the atmosphere.

Pasteur's experiment

French biochemist Louis Pasteur (1864) also conducted an experiment. In his experiment, he boiled hay infusion in a swan-necked flask to kill the microbes and make it sterile. The mouth of the flask was closed. He left the experiment for 18 months.

Observation : Every for over 18 months, Pasteur didn’t find any microorganism in the bottle. But when the mouth of swan-neck was broken, infusion came in contact with air and then microbes appeared quickly.

Conclusion: On the basis of the above observations. Pasteur concluded that microorganisms were created not from inanimate hay infusion but only from their pre-existing forms which might be present in the atmosphere.

Biochemical Origin of Life (Oparin concept)

It is the modern and widely accepted concept of origin of Life. It was put forwarded by Russian scientist Alexander Ivanovich Oparin in 1938 AD. He stated that “Life originated spontaneously from some non-living inorganic compounds in the oceans of primitive earth about 3.3 billion years ago.

Oparin explained the origin of life along with the origin and evolution of earth and its atmosphere of earth had water, methane, ammonia and Cyanamide that underwent a series of reactions and as a result , mixture of biologically important macro molecules like proteins, sugars, nucleic acids etc were formed. As the bio-chemical concept of life is complex phenomenon, Oparin grouped the theory in following three steps.

  1. Chemogeny
  2. Biogeny
  3. Cognogeny

A) Chemogeny

a. Formation of water, ammonia, methane and cynamide

Elements like carbon, hydrogen were most abundant on the primitive earth in the beginning.

These elements exist in the gaseous state due to high temperature.

C + 2H 2 → CH 4 (Methane)

H2 + 20 2 → H 2 O (Water)

N2 + 3H 2 → 2NH 3 (Ammonia)

Oxygen (0 2 ) didn’t occur in free state. All the oxygen were consumed to form water. Such environment is called reducing atmosphere.

b. Formation of hydrocarbon

It is presumed that when the temperature of earth surface was considerably cooled to 100C or even low, the highly reactive free radicals CH and CH 2 condensed to form varieties of saturate andunsaturated hydrocarbons.

CH + CH → C 2 H 2 (Acetylene)

CH 2 + CH 2 → C 2 H 4 (Ethylene)

CH 2 + CH 2 → CH 4 + C (Methane)

c. Formation of Oxy and Hydroxyl derivatives of hydrocarbons

These hydrocarbon reacted with super heated steam Due to unusual bonding property of their carbonoxy and hydroxy derivatives of hydrocarbons such as aldehydes and  ketones were formed.

C 2 H 2 + H 2 O → CH 3 CHO (Acetaldehyde)

d. Formation of carbohydrates, amino acids and fatty acids.

Due to the condensation polymerization, oxidation and reduction of these above molecules such as simple sugar, amino-acids fatty acids were formed.

CH 4 +H 2 0 → Sugars (C 6 H 12 0 6 )

CH 4 + H 2 O + NH 4 → Amino acids

B) Biogeny

a. Formation of nucleic acid

It is presumed that the sugar, phosphate combined together to form nucleotides. A large number of such nucleotides were combined to form nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA.

b. Formation of co-accervates

The nucleic acids along with other macromolecules of primordial soup in the ocean aggregated together and bounded by a water layer to form a colloided' system which is called co-accervates.

c. Formation of primary organisms

These co-accervates started absorbing organic substance from oceanic soup and became multiplying

C) Cognogeny

This involves diversification in Protozoa, Metazoa and Metaphyta

a. Origin of autotrophs

Due to increasing number of heterotrophic in ocean there was shortage of organic nutrients. So organism adapted to different method to obtain food. In course of time some prokaryotic begin to synthesis organic molecules from inorganic substances (chemoautotrophism). Some developed chloroplast made food in presence of sunlight initialing photosynthesis.

b. Oxygen evolution

Due to process of photosynthesis a free oxygen was liberated into the atmosphere. This O 2 brought about a number of changes in the primitive atmosphere. Similarly anaerobic was changed into aerobic respiration and hence ozone layer is formed. In this way presence of free 0 2 and ozone layer made the organism possible to migrate on to land from water.

c. Reducing atmosphere

It is the atmosphere without free oxygen. It was the ancient or primitive atmosphere. The organism was anaerobic.

d. Oxidizing atmosphere

It is the atmosphere with free oxygen. It is the modern or present atmosphere. The organism are aerobic.

chapters.title: Part A - Ch 1: Biomolecules and Cell biology
chapters.content:
Cell: CelI is the basic building unit of life. Cell is the structural and functional unit of life.

Structural - It provide shape and size to living organisms.

Functional - It controls the metabolic activities to keep living organisms alive.

Cell —> Tissue —> Organ —>System —> Organism

Tissue: Group of cells having similar function is called tissue. Group of tissue form organ . Different organ combined together to form system . Different system combine to form living organism.

Discovery of cell:

  1. Robert Hooke (1665) first discovered the cell through the section of cork.
  2. Antony Van Leeweehook discovered bacteria protozoan (1675).
  3. Rudolf Virchow discovered the concept of cell division in 1855
  4. Purkinje and Bohemian introduced term protoplasm for the living content a the cell in 1839.
  5. Kolliker (1857) described mitochondria.
  6. Haeckel (1866) name plastid.
  7. Hofmester discovered chromosome.
  8. Cell theory was given by German Botanist M.I. Schleiden and zoologist Theoder schwann in 1839.
  9. This has made great progress to the modern age.

Cell Theory

The theory proposed by Schwann and Schleinden which state that both plants and animals are made up of with cells is called cell Theory. The basic features of a cell theory are given below.

  1. All living organisms are made up of cell.
  2. All the cells arises from pre-existing cell.
  3. Cell is structural and functional unit of life.
  4. All the cells have similar in chemical composition and similar in metabolic activities.
  5. Growth of living organism takes place by cell division.
  6. They are hereditary units (genes).
  7. They are transferred from parents to offsprings.

The Cell as a self-contained unit

Cell is a small unit which is Autonomous i.e

  1. It is capable to carry the activities independently.
  2. It can carry out different biological process (metabolic activities).
  3. Respiration takes place as a result, energy is release which is stored in the form of A.T.P.

C 6 H 2 O 2 +O 2 (food/glucose) → CO 2 +H 2 O+Energy.  [Respiration]

4. It can regenerate new cells to replace worn out cells.

Cellular Totipotency

The ability of a vegetative part of a plant cell to grow into new plant is called cellular totipotency. Haberlandt (1902) first introduced about the cellular totipotency.

Pollen Grains → Male Gametes

Ovule → Female Gametes

Remaining part except flower is vegetative part.

Steward Experiment to understand the concept of cellular Totipotency

Totipotency of cell can be defined as the capacity of cell/explant to grow into a whole new identical plant. Requirements to produce soma clones of tomatoes are

  1. Explant it is any part of a plant taken out for growing a new plant in special nutrient medium under sterile/aseptic conditions.
  2. Nutrient must have carbon source such as sugar, inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, growth regulators like auxins, cytokinins etc.
  3. Suitable conditions of light and temperature. This is a tissue culture method by which a number of genetically similar plants called can be soma clones can be grown.
  4. The plant let grown are later shifted to nurseries for further development and finally to fields.

Q. Differences between Eukaryotic cells and Prokaryotic cells.

Cell Inclusion: The cytoplasmic content that are non-living and are formed as a result of different metabolic activities are called cell inclusions.

Cell Wall: The cell wall is the outermost plant plant cell.

  1. It is present only in plant cells and lies outside the plasma membrane.
  2. It is made up of complex polysaccharide (Carbohydrate) called cellulose.
  3. Its function is to give strength and rigidity to the cell.
  4. It is non-living.

Cell walls of Plants

  1. May have multiple layers.
  2. Primary cell wall thin and flexible portion of wall made of cellulose and sugar called protein.
  3. Middle lamella: thin layer between primary walls of adjacent cells.
  4. Secondary cel walls found in some cells found between the plasma membrane and primary cell wall.
  5. Impregnated with lignin for strength.

Functions of Cell wall

  1. Prevents enlargement of plant cell.
  2. Play important roles in the absorption transport, secretion of substances in plants.
  3. Provide the plant cell a definite shape and size to strength and rigidity to cell.
  4. Provides protection from physical injury.
  5. Together with Vacuole provides skeletal support.

Cell Membrane

Under electronic microscope cell membrane appears trilaminar and lipoprotenious as it is made up of outer and inner layer by protein white middle one is formed by the bilayer phospholipid molecules. Many molecules of cell membrane have been proposed. Two of them are:

1. Sandwich model

It was proposed by Davson and Danelli. It has following characteristics.

  1. Plasma membrane is lipoprotenious and trilaminar.
  2. It is composed of outer and inner layer of  protein molecules where as middle is composed of bilayer lipids.
  3. Proteins are globular in structure.
  4. Each phospholipid molecules are directed in opposite direction.

2. Fluid Mosaic model

  1. Proposed by Singer and Nicolson.
  2. They describe the model as protein ice berg in the sea of lipid.
  3. Cell membrane (plasma membrane) is a lipoproteins, trilaminar.
  4. Phospholipid is fluidy in nature.
  5. Molecules of phospholipid show two types movement.

Transition Movement (Changing position in same layer)

Flip Flop movement (Changing position in different layer)

6. Protein are globular and is of two types.

Extrinsic protein (peripheral protein) found at surface

Intrinsic protein (Integral protein) found inside surface.

Cell Division: The process in which a mature mother cell divides into two or more than two daughter cell that exist from pre-existing cell is called cell-division. The multiplication and enlargement of a cell is necessary for the growth and development of every organism is due to cell division.

Cell cycle:

The events which takes place between are called cell division to the next cell division is called cell cycle. It explains the history of a cell from beginning of multiple cell division to the next cell division. Cell cycle consists of three main stages:

  1. Interphase
  2. M-phase or mitotic phase
  3. Cytokinesis

1. Interphase

It is the longest phase of the cell cycle. It is metabolically very active. All the necessary material are synthesized so this phase is also called preparatory phase.

It is further divided into 3 sub-stages:

Gap 1(g1): Cell grows, carry out normal functions and replicate their organelles.

Synthesis (S): DNA synthesis

Gap 2(g2): Additional growth

2. Mitosis (M)

It is also known as karyokinesis because there is division of nucleus. It consists of 4 phases

  1. Prophase
  2. Anaphase
  3. Metaphase
  4. Telophase

3.Cytokinesis

Division of cytoplasm is called cytokinesis. It gives rise to two daughter cells these two daughter cells again enters to the interphase.

Types of cell division

A. Amitosis cell division (Direct cell division)

B. Mitosis cell division (Indirect cell division)

C. Meiosis cell division (Reductional cell division)

A. Amitosis cell division (Direct cell division):

It is the direct cell division in which nucleus undergoes direct division followed by cytoplasmic division. It occurs in lower primitive organism of prokaryotic cell.

B. Mitosis cell division (Indirect cell division):

It is a division in which mother cell divide the two daughter cell each having the same number of Chromosome as present to Mother cell.The daughter cells are qualitatively and quantitively similar to their parent cell. It is also known as equational division or somatic cell division. It occurs in vegetative part body.

1) Interphase: Chromosome occur in the form of diffused long, coiled and indistinct chromatin fibre all the necessary material are synthesized and metabolically very active.

2) Mitotic Phase

2.1) Prophase

  1. At early prophase, nuclear membrane and nucleolus are distinct.
  2. Chromatin fibre are long thread like structure.
  3. At middle prophase, nuclear membrane and nucleolus start to disappear. Chromatin fibre are shortened and thickened to form chromosomes.
  4. At late prophase, each chromosome split longitudinally to form sister chromatids.
  5. Nuclear membrane and nucleolus completely disappear.

2.2) Metaphase

  1. Nuclear membrane and nucleolus completely disappear.
  2. Chromosome come to the equatorial region.
  3. Formation of spindle fibre that holds the chromosome at centromere.

2.3) Anaphase

  1. Contraction of spindle fibre.
  2. Centromere splits into two halves.
  3. Each half carries one chromosome and moves towards opposite poles.
  4. At the end of anaphase, two groups of chromosome are formed each group having equal number of chromosome as present in parent cell.

2.4) Telophase

Daughter chromosome reached to their respective poles.

Nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear.

Spindle fibre are completely disappeared.

Some materials are deposited in the middle which help to form cell plate.

3) Cytokinesis

Formation of cell plate takes place and finally divide cytoplasm, this process is called cytokinesis. Two daughter cells are formed which are the exact copies of parent cell.

Significance of Mitosis Cell Division

  1. It helps in growth and development of whole organism.
  2. Replacement of old and damaged cell.
  3. Maintaining genetic stability.
  4. Helps in asexual reproduction.

C) Meiosis Cell Division (Reductional cell division)

  1. It is the type of cell division in which one matured diploid cell produces four haploid daughter cells.
  2. It is also known as reductional cell division because chromosome number get reduced into half as present
  3. in their parent cell.
  4. It takes place in reproductive cells so helps in the formation of gametes.
  5. It causes variation due to crossing over.

Steps followed in Meiosis Cell Division

  1. Interphase
  2. Karyokinesis
  3. Cytokinesis

1) Interphase:

Chromosome occur in the form of diffused, long, coiled and indistinct chromatin fibre all the necessary material are synthesized and are metabolically very active.

2) Karyokinesis: (Division Nucleus)

(Lazy Zebra Perform Disco Dance)

2.1) Meiosis I (V. Imp)

A) Prophase I: It is the longest and complicated phase of Karyokinesis. It is further divided into five parts:

a) leptotene:

  1. Distinct nuclear membrane and nucleolus.
  2. Chromatin fibre are in the form of long-thread-like structure
  3. Gradually chromatin fibre became short and thick and become chromosome.

b) Zygotene:

  1. Pairing of homologous chromosome takes place. This is known as Synapsis.
  2. In each pair, one chromosome come from paternal and one chromosome come from maternal

c) Pachytene:

  1. Chromosome split longitudinally and form tetrad except the centromere
  2. The point of attachment between two sister chromatid is called chiasmata.
  3. Exchange of genetic material takes place between two sister chromatid, this process is called crossing over.

d) Diplotene:

  1. Repulsion force develop between two sister chromatid.
  2. Homologous chromosome begin to move each other. away from each other.
  3. Nuclear Membrane and nucleolus completely disappear.

e) Diakinesis:

  1. Each homologous chromosome repel each other from the point of chiasmata. This process is known as Terminalization.
  2. The chromosome moves towards the periphery.
  3. Spindle fibre start to appear from centriole.

B) Metaphase I

  1. Nuclear membrane and nucleolus completely disappear.
  2. Chromosome come to the equatorial region.
  3. Formation of spindle fibre that holds the chromosome at centromere.

C) Anaphase I

  1. The process of separation of homologous chromosome towards opposite poles is called disfunction.
  2. Chromosome moves towards the opposite poles by the contraction of spindle fibre.
  3. There is no division of centromere.

D) Telophase I

  1. Now the chromosome move to their respective poles.
  2. Spindle fibre completely disappear.
  3. Nuclear membrane and nucleolus re-appear.

E) Cytokinesis I

  1. Immediately after the Telophase I, cytokinesis takes place.
  2. Two daughters are formed by the formation d cell plate.
  3. Nuclear Membrane and Nucleolus re-appear.

2.2) Meiosis II

It is also called the equational cell division because it is quite similar to it. It contains following sub-stages.

A) Prophase II

  1. Chromatin fibre become short and condensed and are clearly visible.
  2. Nuclear Membrane and Nucleolus starts to dissappear.
  3. Spindle fibre start to appear.

B) Metaphase II

  1. Chromosome come to lie at equatorial region.
  2. Nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear.
  3. Spindle fibre holds the chromosome at centromere.

C) Anaphase II

  1. Contraction of spindle fibre.
  2. There is division of Centromere.
  3. Centromere divides into two halves and each halve carry chromosome and move towards the opposite poles.

D) Telophase II

  1. Spindle fibre disappear.
  2. Chromosome move to their respective poles.
  3. Nuclear Membrane and nucleolus reappear.
  4. Gradually there is formation of cell plate.

E) Cytokinesis II

As the cell plate formation is completed at the end of Meiosis cell division four daughter cells are formed.

This four daughter cells are genetically different from each other.

There is variation due to the crossing over.

Significance of Meiosis Cell Division

  1. It takes place in reproduction part which help in sexual reproduction.
  2. It takes place in reproductive cells which help in sexual reproduction.
  3. Due to crossing over genetic variation takes place.
  4. It helps to form gametes (sperm and egg)
  5. It also help in alternation of generation.
