Based on the concepts of normative science.Based on the concept of positive science.

The subject matter of economics means the related area or the scope of the field of study of economics. Though the subject matter of economics is vague and confusing, it can be studied into the following three topics:

1. Representative Approach:

Under this topics subject matter of economics can be discussed under following

three Sub- topics

a) According to Smith, subject matter of economies is centered towards the study of Wealth of nation, it's accumulation and its mobilization

b) According to Marshall, It is the study of mankind in his/her ordinary business life in-order to achieve satisfaction through the material goods.

c) According to Robbins, It is the study of scarcity and choice which have the alternative

uses in order to achieve satisfaction

2. Traditional Approach:

Under this approach, the subject matter of economics is focused towards unlimited wants

and limited means. Because of this all the human does some effort for the satisfaction. These three like wants, effort and satisfaction should rotate or complete the cycle for human. This cycle is as shown as below

Wants

Efforts

Satisfaction

for the continuation of above cycle the human beings should involved in the following activities.

a) Production:

Production is the process of transformation of inputs or factors of production (land, capital, labour, interest and organization) into its output is called production. Under this topics we study various theories like law of variable proportions, laws of return scales, etc

b) Consumption:

The process of satisfying the human wants is called consumption. Under this topic the different theories law of demand, law of diminishing marginal utility, law of minimum satisfaction, etc

c) Distribution:

The process of determining the price of factor of production is called distribution. Under this heading, We study the different theories relating to the price or rewards of factors of production in the form of rent, wages, profit and income.

d) Exchange:

The process of determining the price of goods and services is called exchange. Under this heading, we study the different theory of different markets like profit competition, monopoly ,etc.

e) Government / Public finance:

The branch of economics which deals with the study of government expenditure and income is called public finance. Under this topics, we study about the theory of government expenditure , government revenue, public debt, taxation etc.

3. Modern Concept:

Modern economists have divided the subject matter of economics into two parts. They are a) Micro economics

b) Macro economics

Micro Economics: It studies the economic activities of individual units like individual households, individual farm or individual market. In other words it is the Study single tree among the forest.

Macro Economics: It studies the economic activities of aggregate as a whole like aggregate demand and aggregate supply of all the goods & services in the economy. In other words it is the study of all the trees of forests.

Concept of Positive and Normative economics

The methodology of economic analysis is broadly classified into two categories such as normative economics

Positive Economics:

The concept of positive economic was developed by classical economists such Smith, JB Say, D. Ricardo and modern economist (such as Robbins JM Keynes etc. Positive economics is science of systematic knowledge related to ‘What is’, ‘What was’ or ‘What will’ be. It means Positive economics studies the economic activities

as they happen in reality. It aims to explain the cause and effect of the economic problem but do not tells what is wrong or right and what is desired or not desired. So it is the neutral science. It is also based on scientific analysis and can be studied in numerical form.

Normative Economics:

The concept of normative economics was developed by neo-classical economists like Alfred Marshall, AC Pigou, Cannon, etc. Normative economics is a science of systematic knowledge related to what ought to be, What must be. It mean normative economics studies the economics activities which are not truly happened. It aims to know whether the economic activities are going according to norms and values or not.

So it don't deals with the study of cause and effect of economic problem but it gives the valuable suggestion to reduce the above problem. It is based on norms and values ethics. So it is also called as the ethics science. It means, it says only the good or bad but don’t gives the real focus.

PositiveNormative
Positive economics concerns with 'what is'.Normative economics concerns with 'what should be' or 'what ought to be'.
Positive economics mainly focuses on statistics & factual information.It mainly deals with value judgement of economy.
Positive economics deals with the relationship between cause and effect.Normative economics presents an ideal situation.
In this, we express unemployment is too high in the country.In this, we say poverty is high. So, it should be reduced.
It describes how the economy really works.It describes how the economy should works.
It is the study of economic phenomenas as they are.It is the study of economic phenomenas as they should be.

Concept of Micro and Macro Economics

Micro Economics:

The word micro economics is derived from Greek word ‘Micros’. The meaning of micros is a small unit. So micro economics is the study of the economy of small unit or individual unit. It includes the study of individual consumers, individual firm, individual producer, individual price, individual profit, individual demand, individual wages, individual income and saving. So, it is the study of how individuals make their effective choice, what to produce, what price to charge at the individual firm. So it is also called as price theory of economics.

Importance of Microeconomics:

Recently Microeconomics occupies very important role in the study of economic theory. Some of the importance are as follows:

a) To make the factors payment:

Micro economics plays a very important role for the payments of the contribution made by the factors like land, labour, capital and organization in the form of rent, interest, wages and profit.

b) To make the economic decision:

It helps to make the different plans and policies and programmes in the different headings of economy dominated by public sector. It is also useful in designing the prices of public utilities in an economy.

c) Price determination:

Micro economics also helps to fix the price of goods and Services of the different firms and industry with the help of market demand and market supply.

d) To understand the Working of economy:

Micro economics deals with the study of effective allocation of resources for the producer as well as consumer to obtain the maximum satisfaction.

e) Policy formulation and implementation:

Microeconomics helps the government to prepare and implement the various economic policies such as fiscal policy, monetary policy, trade policy and other development policy in the country.

Macro Economics:

The word macro economics is derived from Greek word ‘Makros’, which means the study of large unit. So macro economics is the study of an economy as a whole or in aggregate form. It studies the behavior of aggregate economic variables such as national income, aggregate demand, aggregate supply, aggregate investment, aggregate consumption, aggregate expenditure, aggregate saving and general price level.

It examines how the general price level is determine and how the resources are allocated for the welfare of the people.

It also focus the level of income and employment in the whole economy. So it is also known as theory of income and employment:

It’s importance are:

Macro economics is useful in several analysis of economic activities of the nation. Some of them are explained below:

a) Formulation of macro-economy policy:

Macroeconomics helps to formulate the aggregate price policy, taxation, monetary policy fiscal policy etc for the rapid growth and development of economy of nation.

b) Solving various social problems:

Macroeconomics is also useful in studying about various problems within the nation Such as unemployment, poverty, inequality, regional disparity, etc. It also implement the various economic policies to remove the above economic problem

c) Measurement of national income:

Macro economics is a very important tools to calculate the national income annually. It makes different analysis and projection on different components of national income. Such as GDP, GNP, PCI of a nation.

d) Economic and monetary policy:

Macro economics also helps to formulate the economic and monetary policy in order to accelerate the rate of economic growth and economic development. It also helps to control the increase in price level (inflation) and decrease in price level (deflation).

e) Helpful in international comparison:

Macro economics also helpful in the companion of different indicators like national income national output, investment patterns, consumption behavior, etc. with the international economy.

chapters.title: Unit 2: Basic Issues of Economics
chapters.content:
Basic Issues of Economics

Factors of Production refers to those goods or services which are required to produce other goods and services. They are also known as inputs. Basically, there are four types of factors of production such as: -

1. Land

2. Labour

3. Capital

4. Organization/Enterprise

1. Land

In narrow console, land is defined as the surface of the earth covered by Soil. But in economic sense land refers to the all the free gifts of nature to the living beings. It includes soil, forest, himalaya, water, air, mines, sunlight etc that is both on the surface and under the surface of the earth.

Features of land are:

Land is an important factor of production. It has unit some unique features which makes the land different from other factors of production .Some of them are discussed below.

1.1) Free gifts of nature

Land cannot be produced or created by man. It is given to free of cost by nature. So, it does not hold any cost of production but it holds market value or price and its volume depends on it’s fertility or productivity of land.

1.2) Fixed in supply

Land is fixed in supply. Efforts of human being cannot change it’s total size or amount. It cannot be extended or contracted by the will of human.

1.3) Land is indestructible

Land is not destroyable. Human beings can destroy the quality of land but not the quantity of fertility of land can be destroyed by efforts of human or by other means. But the total size of land remains constant permanently.

1.4) Passive factor of production:

Land is a passive factor of production. Human efforts are required to activate to make a land a productive factor. It means, land alone cannot produce goods and services unless and until human efforts are made.

1.5) Immobile factor:

Land is a fixed factor. It remains fixed where it is. land is lumpy and indivisible to some cases. Since, it is lumpy and indivisible, it is not transferable from one place to another place.

2. Labour

Generally, labour is a physical or mental capacities of the human beings. But in economics all the human efforts done mentally or physically with the aim of earning income is called labour. Thus, labour is the physical or mental efforts of the human beings in the process of production.

Features of labour:

Labour is used to produce the goods and services through which he /she get the compensation in the form of wages. Some of the features of labour are explained below:-

2.1) Labour is an active factor of production

Labour is the most active and indispensable factor of production. Generally, land and capital remain inactive and fruitless without the use of labour.

2.2) Labour is a perishable factor

Goods and Services can be stored and sold in the future at high price. But labour is perishable and cannot be stored like other factors. If it is not used or if the labourer don’t do a work, the labour is wasted and thus get perishable.

2.3) Labor cannot be separable from laborious

Others factors of production like land and capital can be separated from i's owner. But laborious cannot separate his/her labour from them and send it to different work place. For Eg teachers Cannot perform their teaching activities by sending their knowledge, organs of body and other teaching materials.

2.4) Labour is a mobile factor

Since the land is immobile factor and capital is highly mobile factor, the labour is a mobile factor. It means it can be transferred from one place to another place. But it is less mobile and capital because it has a feeling of love and attachment with the family.

2.5) Refers in efficiency

Different labour have different degrees of working efficiency, working experience skills, training etc. Due to having such different capacities the labour also get different wages and salaries according to their contribution.

3. Capital

In general sense, capital is wealth or money. But in economic sense it refers to all man made artificial goods which are used for the further production of wealth. Machines, tools, buildings, roads, bridges, raw materials etc. are the examples of wealth

Features

Some of the features of capital are as follows:

3.1) Man-made factor

Capital is not automatically created, but it is produced in human efforts as well as other means of production. For eg, Land is not man made but machines, vehicles, etc are man

made factors of production. So, all capitals are made by man.

3.2) Passive factors of production

Since, it is produced by human beings, capital by itself remains unproduced if it is not used by human beings to produce wealth. Unless there is involvement of labor, machines do not give production.

3.3) Most mobile factor

Most of the capitals can be transferred from one place to another or from one use to another. So it is taken as a mobile factor. Various forms of capitals like machinery, money, equipment, vehicles etc are mobile.

3.4)Supply of capital is elastic

Unless land, the supply of capital is elastic. Its supply can be increased or decreased according to the need of the economy. For e:g-the Supply of tools, machinery, etc can be increased or decreased as per society's requirement.

3.5) It depends upon technology

The amount of capital depends upon the level of technology employed by a nation. The more progress is in a country's technology, the more capital is produced in that nation.

4. Organization or Enterprise

It is defined as the collective body of active human resources established for the utilization of factors of production like land, labor and capital in the line of production process. It also organizes co-ordinates all the above factors of production to earn the profit. Some of the features are as follow.

4.1) Collection of people

An organization is established with the help of people. To achieve the goal and target of organization, individual are assigned different role to accomplish various tasks.

4.2) Risk and uncertainty bearing:

Risk and uncertainty is very important for an organization. There is the risk of loss due to uncertain future such as natural calamity change in fashion etc. So organization should have capacity to bear such unexpected condition.

4.3) Profit motive

The main objective of organization is to earn profit and to accumulate wealth. It is also essential for survival as well as expansion far further organization.

4.4) Environment

Organization operates in open environment. It is affected by change in external factors like political, economic, socio-cultural factors, etc.

4.5) Division of labour

Division of labour is very important for the organization to be flourished. It is possible under the basis of potential training, skills of the labour in different units or departments.

Concept of Scarcity and Choices

Introduction

Scarcity and choice are the basic problem in economics. This concept was developed by economists Lionel Robbins in 1932 AD. Human wants are unlimited but resources to meet them are limited which creates the problem in any economy and all as economic problem.

Concept of Scarcity

Scarcity refers to the condition of insufficiency where the human beings are incapable of fulfilling their desires in sufficient manner. In other words, the scarcity in economic sense is that the commodity becomes scarce to satisfy the desire of individuals, society, nation as well as entire world.

As the human wants are unlimited. We may satisfy some of our wants but soon new wants arises continuously with the multiplication. Thus, scarcity explains the relationship between unlimited wants and limited resources and the problem like poverty, inequality, unemployment and so on.

Concept of choice

Choice is the process of efficient selection of few goods or wants from the bundle of goods or wants. As the human beings are suffered from the lack of resources but they have to fulfill their unlimited demands, there is the problem of choice. So, they are unable to fulfill their unlimited desires. During the fulfillment of their unlimited desires, some desires should be sacrificed to satisfy some other desire. Hence the people postponed less urgent wants to satisfy the more urgent wants at first. for eg, if a boy has the desire of purchasing the economics book, he should sacrifice to visit cinema hall. Thus, economic problem because of unlimited wants and scarce resources is as shown below chart

Opportunity cost is defined as the second best alternative that has been sacrificed by the consumer or producer by taking an economic decision. In other words, it is also defined as the next best alternative that has been for gone. for eg, student has 3 hours time with him or her and there are two alternatives first is, completing the economic homework and second one is watching the movie in QfX Cinema hall. If a student decides to do homework its opportunity cost is the entertainment that could be received by watching movie. If he/she goes for movie it's opportunity cost is doing his/her homework.

Allocation of resources

Allocation of resources means the scientific and appropriate management utilization of scarce resources in the production, distribution of exchange. It deals with how much of the resources in which and what sector. It is the basic problem of every because all of the economic have limited resources but unlimited desires and wants. The main objective of allocation of resource is to achieve the maximum satisfaction from the utilization of lack of resources. In order to allocate the resources the following problem should be considered:

1) What to produce

This means what types of and what amounts of goods and services to produce by how much or in what quantities. Every wants of individual cannot be satisfied by the producers. So. the producer, society and even the nation must choose the best alternatives from above in order to satisfy the public desires in the market.

2) How to produce

The second problem related to allocation of resources is concerned with the methods of production. It means either to use labour intensive technology or to use capital intensive technology. So, the decision should be made on the basis of his/her capacity or available resources.

3) Whom to produce

Due to the Scarcity of resources the producer cannot satisfy all the wants of the consumers. So decision have to be taken concerning with how many of each wants are to be satisfied. For eg. whether the production is for teenager or for middle age group or for old age group. In this way the scarce resources should be allocated and should be decided whom to Produce goods and services.

4) Sector development

While allocating the resources, nation should give equal priority for the balance development to all the sectors such as primary sector (agriculture), Secondary sector (Industry) and service sector (banking and official sector) of the whole economy.

Concept of Production Possibility Curve (PPC)

As the human wants are unlimited but resources to meet this wants are limited or scarce .This creates problem of choice and this problem can be explained graphically with the help of production possibility Curve. A production possibility refers to the alternative combination of goods and services that could be produce with all the available resources within a specific Period of time. The concept of PPC was developed by P.A. Samuel Son. According to him PPC is that curve which represents the maximum amount of pair of goods that can be both produced with in an economy by the available resources and technique.

In other words, It is the graphical representation of various combination of goods and services that an economy can produce with the full use of the given resources and state of technology.

ASSUMPTIONS

The concept of PPC is based on the following Assumptions:

1) Economy is producing only two goods.

2) There is full employment of resources.

3) Production technology is given and constant.

4) Factors of production are fixed.

5) Time period is given or it is for specific period.

6) The concept of PPC can be explained by the following table and graph

Possibilities/CombinationsConsumer goods (000)Capital goods (000)
A015
B114
C212
D39
E45
F50

The above table shows that the producer can produce a maximum of consumer goods and no capital goods at the combination ‘F’. It is because of the scarcity of resources. In this way the producer select the different combinations like A, B, C, D, E for the production of consumer goods and capital goods.

The above table can be represented by the below graph.

In the above figure, the consumer goods and capital goods are measured along x-axis and y-axis respectively. Combination ‘A’ represents the production possibility of 15000 of capital goods and no consumer goods. Similarly, point B, C, D, E and F represents the different combinations of capital goods and consumer goods. So ‘A’ ,’F’ is a PPC.

In the figure, the point G represents that it is a inefficient point because the resources are not fully utilized. The point 'H' represent that it is unattainable point because the producer is suffered by scarcity of resources. Thus, the consumer has to choose the possible possibilities on the PPC in order to produce goods and services.

Goods & Services

Goods are all those tangible things on commodities that are used to satisfy human desires. In other words, all the commodities having utility are called goods. For eg foods, clothes, golds, silvers etc are the goods.

Services are the human works, efforts which are intangible but satisfy the human wants. For eg, doctor’s work, lawyer’s work, teacher’s work, performing musics & dances, etc are example of Services.

Types of goods

1) Normal goods:

Those goods are normal goods whose quantity demanded increases as the income of the consumer increases and vice versa. It means there is the positive relationship between income of the consumers and demand of such goods. All the daily consumable goods are normal goods.

2) Inferior goods:

The goods are inferior goods whose quantity demanded increases with the decreasing income of the consumer and vice - versa. It means there is negative relationship between income of the consumer and quantity demand of such goods. For eg: Black & White Tv, Street food & clothes etc are inferior goods.

3) Giffen goods:

Giffen goods are special types of inferior whose quantity demanded increases with the increasing price and vice-versa. This types of goods are generally consumed by the poor people of remote areas. It was firstly developed by Economist Sir Robert Giffen. It has positive relationship between price of such goods and quantity demand.

4) Substitute goods:

The goods which partly or fully satisfy the same needs of consumers are called substitute goods. In other words, these are the goods which can be used in place of each other. For eg, tea & coffee, coke & Pepsi, jell pen & ink pen etc. In such goods, there is the positive relationship between price of the commodity and the quantity demand of its substitute.

5) Complementary goods.

The goods which are used together to satisfy a want is called complementary goods. In other Words, the goods which are useless in the absence of another is called complementary goods. For eg, Pen & ink, Shoes & shock, car & petrol etc. In such goods, there is the negative relationship between price of the commodity and quantity demand of its compliment.

6) Private goods

The goods which are produced by and owned by private individual or enterprises is called private goods. In other words, the private goods also defined as the goods having the features of rivalry and excludability.

7) Public goods

The goods which are owned by society and government and also common to all are called public goods. In other words, public goods are also defined as goods having the features of non-rivalry and non-excludability. For eg: roads, bridges, parks etc.

Shifts in PPC (Production Possibility Curve)

The movement of PPC from its initial position to inward (downwards) and outward (Upward) position due to the change in technology, capital, skill of labour, raw materials, etc is called shifts in PPC. Causes of outward Shift in PPC:

a) Due to improvement in productivity of labor through training & education

b) Due ta the availability of her raw materials in large quantity.

c) Due to technological progress.

d) Due to the available of natural materials (land) for the production in large quantity.

Causes of inward shift in PPC

a) Backwardness in technology

b) Shortage of natural resources

c) Lack of training & skill development programs to the labor

d) Decrease in involvement of capital, machinery and equipments.

e) Decrease in size of population due to war, emigration.

The shift in PPC can be shown by following graph:

In the above figure, the curve A F is the Initial PPC which is plotted due to the various combination of two goods and services produced by an economy or producer by the available resources & technology. If the resources as well as technology is positively change the original PPC shift towards right i.e. called outward shift which is denoted by A’ F’ curve. Similarly, if the resources and technology are negatively changed, the original PPC will shift towards left i.e. called inward shift which is denoted by A” F” in figure.

Concept of GDP, GNP

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is defined as the total market value of all the final goods and services produced within a geographical boundary of country during a year. In other words, it is also calculated by muliplying all the goods and Services produced within a country by their respective price in a year.

GDP = P1Q1 + P2Q2 +…….PnQn

Where,

P1= Price of first commodity

Q1= Quantity of first commodity. It is equal to price of second commodity and so on.

Features of GDP

a) GDP is a market/money value of goods services

b) GDP includes only currently produced goods and services.

c) GDP includes goods and services produced with the country.

d) GDP includes only the money value of final goods.

e) It excludes transfer payment.

GNP

Gross National product (GNP) is defined as the market value of all the final goods and services produced during a year by domestically owned resources. In other words it is also defined as the total market value of all the final goods and services produced in a country + net factor income from abroad (NFIA)

GNP = GDP + NFIA

Features of GNP

a) GNP is a market/money value of goods and services.

b) GNP includes only currently produced goods and services.

c) GNP includes only the money value of final goods.

d) GNP includes goods and services with the country

e) It excludes transfer payment.

chapters.title: Unit 3: Demand & Supply
chapters.content:
Introduction

Economy to defined as an integrated and organized activities related to the production, distribution, exchange and consumption of goods and services that are held in a Country It means all the economic problem like production, distribution exchange and consumption will be addressed by an economy.

Different types of economy are practiced on the different countries. They are as follows:

1) Market economy:

It is also known as open economy or free economy or capitalist economy. It is also defined as the economic system where the economic problems related to production, consumption, distribution employment etc are expected to be solved by two market forces, demand and supply. In market economy private sector is consider to be backbone of economy. Government plays only the role of monitor and supervisor of the economy. This type of economy is adopted by the countries like USA, Germany Australia, Italy, etc.

Features of Market Economy:

a) It involves only private sector. It means in market economy all the economic activities are carried out by private sector

b) Existence of market mechanism. It means such economy the prices of goods and Services are determined by the demand and supply of one related goods & services

c) In market economy consumers are free to consume the goods and services. They can utilize and purchase their desired amount at the market price. There is no any compulsion to use the goods and Services on the basis of procedure activities

d) No government control in such economy or intervention. Economic activities are managed and controlled by the market forces. Government only act as facilitator.

e) Competition, in such market there is the freedom of choice. So it creates the competition among the workers to get the job, among producer to attract the consumer and aong the consumers to get the quality goods.

2) Socially / centrally planned Economy

Socialist economy is also called a centrally-planned economy. In this type of economy are owned and operate by the government. This economy plays active role and give focus on social welfare. Economy system is less practiced in the world countries like Cuba, North Korea, Syria etc are practicing such economy.

3) Mixed /Dual Economy

Mixed economy is also called Dual Economy. In this economy there is the involvement of both private and public sector and various economic activities are carried by them. Almost all the developing countries are following such economy to uplift the economic development of their country. Such economy is practicing in the Countries like India, China, Nepal, Brazil and Bhutan.

Desire & demand

In general sense, desire & demand are synonyms. But in real sense, desire means the quantity of goods and services then an individual is just willing to have or it is their wish of an individual to have something. Demand is such an effective desire of an individual which are backed up by willingness. to pay and ability to pay for the specific time of period. For example, if poor person has a desire to purchase a car, it is only just a wish because he is not able to pay the price. If a rich person has a  desire to purchase a car, it is his demand he has an ability to pay and willingness to pay at that situation.

According to above definition, demand includes following factors:

a. Effective desire of the commodity.

b. Ability to pay.

c. Willingness to pay.

d. Per period of time.

e. Quantity of commodity.

Types of Demand (Indirect & Direct)

a. Price demand

b. Income demand

c. Cross demand

Direct demand refers to the quantity demanded of various goods & services which are directly consume or used by the consumers. This demand is directly effected by price, Income and price of a related goods.

Types of direct demand are:

a. Price demand

It refers to the various quantities of a commodity which a consumer would purchase at various price level of the commodity. It shows the inverse relationship between price and the quantity demanded. This relationship can be shown by hypothetical table and graph.

In the above figure, the price of the commodity and the quantity demand of that commodity are measured along y-axis and x-axis respectively DD’ is the demand curve which shows the negative relation between price of the commodity and the quantity demand of that commodity, other things remain same.

b.Income Demand Income demand refers to the various quantities of a commodity which a consumer would purchase of various level of the commodity It shows the positive income relationship between income and the quantity demanded of normal goods. Similarly, it shows the negative relationship between income level & quantity demand of interior goods. which can be shown by the following table & graph.

In the above figure (i) the demand curve DD' represents the positive relationships between the income level of the consumer and quantity demand of normal goods. Similarly in figure (ii) the demand curve DD’  represent the inverse relationship between the income level of the consumer & quantity demand of inferior goods.

Cross demand Cross demand refers to the quantity demand of the related goods (substitutes and complement goods) which a consumer would purchase at the different price level of that two goods. It shows the relationship between the demand of one commodity and the price of other related commodity. It can be studied further two heading.

Substitute goods

In substitute goods the demand of one Commodity is directly related to the price of Its relative goods. If the price of Coke is increased then the quantity demand of Pepsi will be increased.

Complementary goods.

In complementary goods there is negative relationship between the price of goods with the quantity demand of the related goods. For eg if the price of shoe is increased the quantity demand of its complement. i.e. Shocks is deceased

Indirect/Derived demand

Joint Demand

Composite Demand

Indirect demand refers to the various quantities of commodity that can be used for multiple purpose or can be use for single specific work. For eg, demand of water & electricity, demand of tea dust, sugar, milk, Water for the purpose of cup of tea are indirect demand.

a. Joint demand

Joint demand refers to the demand of several goods. that can be jointly used for specific purpose. For eg, demand far car & petrol, pen and ink etc

b. Composite demand

Composite demand refers to demand of those goods which can be used for multiple purpose. For eg, demand for water & electricity.

Determinants / Factors of Demand

The factors or the elements that increase or decrease the demand of the commodity is known as determinants of demand. The sum of the determinants of demand are as follows:

a. Price of commodity

b. Income of the consumer

c. Price of related goods

d. Taste & preference of the consumer

e. Size of population

f. Advertisement

g. Seasons

h. Culture and tradition

Price of Commodity

The price of commodity is the major determinant of demand Other things remaining same, when the price of commodity increases the quantity demanded for that commodity will decrease and vice-versa. It means there is the negative relationship between price and the quantity demand of commodity.

Income of the consumer

It is another important determinant of quantity demanded for a product. At a higher level of income demand will be high for luxurious & normal goods and low for infall goods and vice versa.

Price of related goods

If two products tea & coffee are substitute goods, then there will be a positive positive effort of a Change in price of coffee on the demand for tea. That means an Increase in the price of coffee leads to an increase in demand of tea & vice versa.

Taste & preference of consumers

If taste and preferences of consumers are changed in favor of a particular good, then the demand for that good will be higher.

Size of population

Demand of goods will be higher in case of larger population. If the size of population is lower then demand will be lower.

Demand function / Equation

Demand function is a mathematical expression that shows the relationship between demand for commodity with it's determinants. It can be written in the form of equation

D = F (P, Y, Pxy, Po, Ad, S, T)

Where,

D = Demand

F =  Functional relationship

P = Price of commodity

Y = Income of the consumers

Pxy = Price of related goods (substitute and compliment)

Po = Size of population

Ad = Advertisement

S = Season & climate

T = Tasa & Preference

Law of Demand  [ V. IMP ]

Law of Demand states that, there is the negative relationship between price of commodity and its quantity demanded. This law was developed by an economists. Alfred Marshall to explain the relationship between price and quantity demanded of any product. He states that, “Other things remaining same the quantity demanded increases with the fall in price and vice versa.

Symbolically the statement of law of demand can be written as

Px(Increase)   Dx(Decrease)

Px(Decrease)   Dx(Increase)

Where,

Px  = Price of X Commodity

Dx = Demand of X Commodity

Assumptions The law of demand is based on the following assumptions

a. No change in the income of the consumer.

b. No change in price of related goods.

c. No change in taste, preferences fashion of the consumer.

d. No change in size of population.

e. No change in season & climate.

The law can be explained by the following table and graph.

The above table shows that there is an inverse relationship between price of commodity and its quantity demand. At the rupees 5 the quantity demand of commodity is 3 units. On increasing the price from Rs 10-15, the quantity demanded decreases from 2-1 unit which can be shown by following graph.

In the above figure, quantity demand of commodity and its price are measured/plotted in x-axis and y-axis respectively. The demand curve DD’ is formed by the combination of different points a, b, and c. The demand curve DD’ shows an inverse relationship between price and quantity demand of commodity as it is downward slopping.

Exceptions / Limitations of law of Demand

According to the law of demand, there is an inverse relationship between the price and the quantity demand of commodity. But this law doesn’t holds true far all the goods, persons, times, play and environment. During this situation the law of demand doesn’t hold true, it is known as exception or limitations of law of demand. These exceptions can be explained as below:

a. Basis or necessary or neutral goods

The law of demand is not applicable in the case of basic or necessary goods like salt, medicines, water, etc. The demand for such goods remains unchanged for all levels of price. This is against you law of demand.

b. Prestigious goods

Prestigious goods are those goods which are related to the prestige of consumers such as gold, silver, precious stones, rare paintings etc. So, demand for Such goods increase even the price of such goods increases as they offer prestige to the consumers. It is also against the law of demand.

c. Change in taste and preferences

If the consumers tastes and preference are changes in favour of all particular goods, then demand for such goods increases even at the same price or the consumer will be ready to pay even higher price to purchase the same quantity of goods. For eg, the demand for a cone of ice-cream increases in the summer even at higher price.

d. Ignorance of consumer

If the consumer is not aware of the competitive price of the same commodity, he purchases mare of the commodity even at higher price. It is because high place commodity are generally considered as superior in quality. Such attitude and ignorance of consumer makes the law of demand ineffective.

e. Price of shortage of expectations.

If the consumer feel that there is going to be the shortage of a commodity in near future or price is going to be rise then they demand more goods & services at present paying higher prices due to the fear of further rising price. It is also against the law of demand.

Generally, the demand curve slopes downWard from left to right because of the following reasons:

a. Income effect

It is the effect on demand for goods due to the change in real income of the consumers as a result of change in the price of goods. The income effect simply indicates that at a lower price one can afford more of the goods and vice-versa. In other words, decreasing in price will increase the purchasing power of income. So, the consumer is able to buy more of the commodity.

b. Substitution effect

It is the effect in the demand of a cheaper commodity in place of expensive one due to change in price of substitute goods. This effect suggest that at a lower price the consumer substitute the cheaper goods with the expensive goods. for eg, a decline in price of Wai Wai noodles, it increase purchasing power of consumer making them able to buy more of them if the price of Aaha noodles is same.

c. Diminishing marginality

It is the satisfaction that drives after the consumption of additional units of the goods and services which is always decreasing. So, The consumers purchase a demand the goods having less satisfaction only at the lower price. Due to this, the demand curve slopes downward.

d. Multiple uses of goods.

There are some goods and services which can be put into several uses. When the price of such goods increases, the consumer reduce the use of that goods. For eg, electricity can be used for lightning, cooking, heating, etc when the price of electricity rises, its consumption may be restricted only to lightning. As a result, the demand for electricity is decreased.

e. Entry of new consumers

As The will be fall in the price of a commodity, some new consumers who didn’t use to buy it at previous price begin to purchase it. Consequently, the demand of the goods increases with the fall in price and vice-versa. Due to this, the entry of new consumers create the sloping of demand curve downward.

Demand Schedule & Curve

Demand Schedule is the tabular  representation of various quantities of goods & services demand by the consumer at different price level.

Demand Curve is the graphical representation of the various quantities of goods and services demanded by the consumers at different price level or it is also defined as the graphical representation of the demand schedule.

Types of Demand Schedule & Demand Curve

Individual Demand Schedule

Individual demand Schedule is the tabular representation of various quantities of goods & services demanded by an individual at different price level.

Individual Demand Curve.

It is the graphical representation of the various quantities of the commodities demanded by an individuals at different price level. These can be Shown by Following table & graph

The above demand schedule is the individual demand schedule for different price level of rice and different quantity demand of rice by Ram.

The above demand curve shows the individual demand curve of Ram at different price level for various quantities of rice. The demand curve DD’ is downward sloping as the price level is increasing the quantity demand far rice is decreasing

Market Demand Schedule and Curve

It is the tabular representation of the various quantities of commodity demanded by the market (two or mare consumers) at different price level.

Market Demand Curve

It is the graphical representation of the various quantities of commodity demanded at the market at different price level. Both market demand schedule and market demand curve is obtained by the summation of individual demand schedule and individual demand curve. Market demand schedule de market demand curve are as shown below:

The above market demand schedule shows that when the price of the commodity falls, its market demand rise. For eg. When the price is Rs 50 the market demand is 15 units. Similarly, when the price is falling up to Rs 30 the market demand is rising by 45 units.

In the above figure, quantity demand of Ram and Shyam and price are plotted in x-axis and y-axis respectively. DDR refers to demand curve of Ram, DDS refers to the demand curve of Shyam and DDM refers to the market demand curve which is obtained by the summation of demand of Ram & Shyam. So, the market demand curve is the horizontal summation of individual demand curve at different price level and different quantities of Commodity.

Change in Quantity Demanded / Movement Along Demand Curve

Movement along demand curve can be defined as the state of increase or decrease in the quantity demanded due to fall or use in price, all other factors remaining the same. In Other words, change in the quantity demanded due to the change in price only is called movement along demand curve. Movement is always along the same demand curve i.e. no new demand curve is drawn. Its types are explained below:

Contraction along demand curve

Movement along the demand curve is said to be contraction when the quantity demanded for a commodity decreases due to rise in price, other things remaining same. It is also known a decrease in quantity demanded. The consumers moves upward along the same demand curve during this situation.

Expansion along demand curve

Movement along demand curve is said to be expansion when the quantity demanded / commodity increases due to fall in price. Other things remaining same. It is also known as increase in quantity demanded. The consumer's moves downward along the same demand curve during this situation. The concept of movement along demand curve is as shown below

The above figure x-axis represents quantity demanded and y-axis represent price of the commodity. DD1 is the demand curve which is obtain by plotting the different combinations of price and quantity demand. Rs.10 and 10 units are the initial price and the corresponding quantity demanded and shown by the point A on demand Curve. When the price is rising up to Rs.15, the quantity is decreasing from 10-5 units which is shown by point C. It is the contraction in demand curve. Similarity, if the price falls to Rs 5, the quantity demand increase un to 15 units which is shown by paint ‘B’.  It is expansion along demand curve.

Shift in demand Curve (Change in Demand)

Shift in demand curve refers to the change in quantity demanded due to change in various factors of demand except price. It is also known as change in demand. The shift in demand curve is shown by drawing of new demand curve. It's types are explained below:

Rightward shift / Increase in demand

Rightward shift in demand curve refers to the more demand of the commodity at the same price due to the positive change in the factors of demand. It is also known as increase in demand. In this situation, the initial demand curve shift rightward. The reason for rightward Shift in demand curve are as follows: Increase in size and population

  • Increase in taste & preferences
  • Increase in price of substitute goods
  • Decrease in price of complementary goods
  • Increase in income

Leftward Shift / Decrease in demand

Leftward Shift in demand curve refers to the less demand of the commodity at the same  price due to the negative change in factors of demand. It is also known as decrease in demand. In this situation the initial demand curve shift leftward. The reason of leftward shift in demand are:

  • Decrease in Income
  • Decrease in population
  • Decrease in taste and preferences
  • Decrease in price substitute goods
  • Increase in price of complementary goods

The above topic can be shown in following figures

In the above figure x-axis represents the quantity demand for the commodity and the y-axis represent the price of the commodity. The demand curve DD2 is initial demand curve in which the initial quantity demand is 10 unit. When the income of the consumer is increased, the initial demand curve shift towards right at the same price Rs 10 and represented by demand curve, DD3 which is rightward shift in demand. Similarly, when the income of the consumer is decreased the initial demand curve seems towards left at same price and represented by DD1, which is leftward shift in demand.

Difference between Movement along Supply Curve and shift in Supply Curve

Factor causing shift in Demand

A normal demand curve shifts either left or right due to the change in various factors of demand except the price Some of the major factors which cause the shift in demand curve are explained as below:

a. Change in income of the consumers.

b. Change in size of population.

c. Change In taste & preferences.

d. Change in price of related goods.

e. change in advertisement.

f. Change in Season.

g. Change in income distribution

h. Consumer's future expectation

i. Availability of credit

Change in income of the consumers

The demand for any commodity changes along with the change in income of the consumers. If there is an increase in the income of the consumer, demand for normal goods increases and the demand curve shifts toward right and vice- versa.

Change in size of population

The demand for any commodity changes along with the change in size of population. If there is an increase in the size of population. The demand for goods & services will increase and the demand curve shift towards right and vice-versa.

Change in taste and preferences

the demand for any commodity also changes along with the change in taste & preference of the consumers. If the consumers taste and preferences increases towards the new goods then it increases the demand for that goods leaving the old goods and vice-versa.

Change in consumer's future expectation

The demand for commodity changes along with the change in future expectation of further rise in price by the consumers. In this situation, the consumer demand the more quantity of goods to escape from the pinches of high price and the demand curve shift rightward where as in the inverse the demand curve shift leftward.

Availability of credit

The demand for the commodity also depends on the easy availability of credit system in the market. If there is the availability of credit system to buy the goods and services, there will be increase in demand of those goods and services. causing the rightward shift of demand curve. If there is lack of credit facility, the demand curve will be shifted to leftward.

Concept of Supply

In general sense, supply is the selling of goods and services. But in economic sense, supply is the quality of goods and services that the sellers, suppliers are willing  to and able to sell to the market at different price level for unit of time.

The quantity supplied of goods and services is directly related to price. It means higher the price will be the quantity supplied and vice-versa.

Supply function

Supply function is the mathematical relationship between quantity supplied and its determinant. Mathematically, It can be explained as Sx = F ( Fx, Pf, T, G …..)

where,

Sx = Supply of x commodity

F = function relationship

Fx = Price of x commodity

Pf = Price of factors of production or cost production

T = Technology

G = Government policy (tax policy)

Determinants of supply

Price of the product

One of the major determinant of quantity supplied is price of the same product other things remaining the same, higher the price, higher will be the quantity supplied.

Cost of production

It also determines the quantity supplied.

Law of Supply (imp)

Law of supply shows the positive relationships between the price and quantity supplied of good and services. This law states that, “Other things remaining same, the quantity supplied increases with the rise in price and vice-versa.” Symbolically the law of supply can be written as

P(Increase), Qs(Increase)  & P(Decrease), Qs(Decrease), other things remaining same

Where ,

P= Price of commodity

Qs = Quantity Supplied

This law is based on the following assumption

a. No change in number of firms

b. No change in technology

c. No change in cost of production

d. No change in tax and subsidy policy of the government

e. No change in price expectations

The law of supply can be explained with the help of below table and graph

The above table shows that different combination of price of the commodity and its quantity supplied. On increasing the price from Rs 10 - 30, the quantity supplied is also increasing from 5 units - 15 units. Which shows the positive relationship between price and quantity supplied. The law of supply can be shown by below figure.

In the above figure, the price and the quantity supplied are shown in y-axis and x-axis respectively. SS’ is a supply curve which obtained by plotting different combinations of price and quantity supplied with point A,B and C. This shows that the price and quantity supplied has positive relationship which support the law of supply.

There is decrease in cost of production, it increase the quantity supplied.

Number of firms

The number of firms in the Industry also determine the quantity supplied. If there are more number of firms in the industry, they produce more goods & services and supply will be more.

Development of infrastructure

If the basic infrastructures like road, transport and communication are well developed it helps to Increase the Supply.

State of technology

New technology helps to increase the supply whereas the old and outdated technology reduces the supply.

Exception / Limitation of Law of Supply

The law of supply states that increase in price raises the supply and vice-versa.

a. Auction sale

The law of supply states that quantity supplied increases with increase in price and vice-versa. But this law doesn’t hold true in case of auction sale.

b. Perishable goods

Goods which have very short life time and become useless after some time are called perishable gods. Such goods must be supplied in the market at the night time whatever be it's price.

c. Agricultural goods

The law of supply is isn’t applicable in agriculture goods. The Supplies of such goods are governed by seasonal factors rather than price

d. Supply of labor

The supply of labor (supplied by laborer) does not follow the law of supply. Anyone supplies labor oat any market wage  trade.

e. At the time of depression

Depression is that situation in the economy in which all the economic activities like production, employment.

Supply Schedule and Curve

Supply schedule is defined as the tabular representation of various combination of quantity supplied of a commodity at different price level.

Supply Curve is defined as the graphical representation of the various combinations of quantity supplied of a commodity at different price level. It is also defined as the graphical representation of the supplied schedule.

It's types are:

a. Individual supply schedule and curve: Individual supply schedule is the tabular representation of the various combinations of quantity supplied of a commodity at different price level by an individual procedures.

c. Individual supply curve: Individual supply curve is the graphical representation of the various combinations of quantity supplied of a commodity at different price level by an individual producers.

Individual supply schedule and supply curve are shown below:

In the above schedule there are different combination between price and quantity supplied of commodity by Ram at different level which is shown by A, B and C. It shows that when the price of commodity is increased from 10-20, the quantity supply by Ram also from 5-15 units. This combinations can be represented by below graph.

In the above graph, the price and the quantity supplied by Ram are represented by y-axis & x-axis respectively. SS’ is the individual supply curve of Ram which is obtained by plotting the different combinations of price and quantity supplied of Ram at paint A, B and C. It shows that he relation price and quantity supplied has positive relation.

Market supply schedule and curve

Market Supply Schedule

It is the tabular representation of the various quantities of commodity supplied at different price level by two or more producers.

Market Supply Curve

It is the graphical representation of the various quantity of commodity supplied at different price level by two or more consumers producers.

Both market supply schedule and market supply curve are obtained by the Summation of individual supply schedule and supply curve - They are shown below:

The above market supply schedule shows that when the price of the commodity falls, it’s Supply also falls, when the price is 50 market supply is 45 units. Similarly when price is 30 then the market supply is decreased by 15 Units.

In the above given figure, quantity supply of Ram and Shyam are plotted in X-axis and Y-axis respectively. Rs refers to supply curve of Ram, Ss for Shyam and SSM to the market supply Curve. It shows the positive relationship between price and quantity supplied

Change In Supply

It is defined as the quantity supplied of any commodity due to the change in its prices or change in determinant of supply. It can be studied into two further headings

a. Movement along Supply curve

b. Shift in Supply

Movement along supply curve

Movement along supply curve is defined as the state of increase or decrease in the quantity supplied of a commodity due to increase or decrease in its price, other things remaining same. It is also known as change in quantity Supplied. In this

situation, the producer moves either upwards or downwards along the same supply curve i.e. no new supply curve is drawn It consists of following headings.

Extension along supply curve

Movement along supply curve is said to be extension when the quantity supplied of a commodity increases with the increase in its price, other things remaining same. It is also known as increase in quantity supplied. In This situation, the producer moves upward along the same supply curve

Contraction along supply curve

Movement along Supply curve is Said to be contracts When the quantity supplied of a commodity decrease with the decrease in its price, other things remains same is also known as decrease in quantity Supplied. In this situation, the producer moves downward along the same supply curve.

It can be explained by the following figures

In the above given figure, price and quantity supplied of a commodity are represented at y-axis & x-axis respectively. SS’ is the Supply curve. When the price of commodity is Rs 10 then the quantity supplied is 20 units which is shown by point A. If the price is increased from 10-15, the quantity supplied by the seller also increase from 20-30 units which is extension in supply curve from A-B. When the price is decrease from Rs 10-5, the quantity supplied by the seller also decreases from A-C which is contraction in supply curve.

Shift in supply

Shift in supply is the state of increase or decrease in the supply of Commodity due to the change in determinants of supply except the price. It is also known as change in supply in which the new Supply curve is drawn either rightwards or leftwards farm its initial position. Its types are as follows:  Rightward shift / Increase in supply

The state of increase in supply due to the favourable change in the determinants of supply except price is called as rightward shift in supply. In this situation, the new supply curve is drawn towards right from its original position. the causes of rightward shift are:

  • Decrease in cost of production.
  • Decrease in government tax rate policy.
  • Increase in number of firms.
  • Use of improved new technology.

Leftward shift / Decrease in supply

Leftward shift is the state of decrease in supply due to unfavourable change in the determinant of supply except price. In this situation new supply curve is drawn towards left from its original position. The cause of it are:

  • Increase in cost of production.
  • Increase in government tax rate policy.
  • Decrease in number of times.
  • Use of old outdated technology.

Shift in supply can be shown by following figure.

In the above figure the price and the quantity supplied of the commodity are represented in y-axis & x-axis respectively. When the price is Rs.10, the quantity supplied is 20 unit which is shown by point B in the original Supply curve SS2. If the any determinants (cost of production, government tax pay) is decreased, the quantity supplied will be increased which is shown by the new supply curve SS3 i.e . rightward shift. If the any determinants of supply are increased the quantity supply will be decrease which is shown by the supply curve SS1 ie leftward shift in supply.

Interaction Between Demand & Supply

Demand & supply are the two major Instrument of the market economy. The equality between quantity demand and quantity supply is known as interaction between demand and supply or market equilibrium. The price which is determined by the market equilibrium is called equilibrium price and the quantity which is determined by the market equilibrium is called equilibrium quantity. The concept of market equilibrium can be explained by the help of below schedule and graph.

Factors Causing Shift in Supply

There are various factors which bring increase or decrease in supply. Same of major factors are described:

a. Cost of production

Cost of production includes price of raw materials, wages and salaries of the workers, cost of energy and so on. If the overall cost of production increases, then it produces production & there by supply. Hence, decrease in costs of production increases the supply and the supply curve shifts towards right from its original position.

b. Number of films in the industry

An industry includes several firm in it. If the number of firms increases, supply and the supply curve shifts towards right and vice-versa.

c. Fiscal policy of the government tax and subsidy

If the government imposes high rate of technology on goods and services. It reduces the supply and supply curve shift towards left and vice versa

d. Change in technology

The technology used by the producing firm may be modern or outdated. Use of modern technology increases output and it shifts the supply curve towards right and vice-versa.

e. Infrastructures

Well-developed infrastructure like road, transport and other basis facilities help to increase the supply and the supply curve shift towards right and vice-versa.

chapters.title: Unit 9: Natural resources of Nepal
chapters.content:
Forest resources are of immense important to develop the Nepalese economy. Justify it with its importance.

Among all the natural resources, forest resources stand in the second position for the economic development as well as to maintain environmental balance in Nepal. It has played a multi dimensional role in our daily life. Nepal is very rich in its forest resources forest contributes about 15% of GDP of Nepal. It is also responsible for the timely rainfall and development of agriculture .It provides direct and indirect employment opportunities to many labour in forest-based industries. It is said 42% of area should be covered by forest for ecological balance. However, forest has occupied around 44.7% (including 40.36% forest and 4.38% shrubs) of the total area of Nepal by the end of fiscal year 2015/16.

Its benefits are as follows:

a. Major source of energy.

b. Source of industrial raw materials.

c. Generates more employment opportunities.

d. Preservation of wildlife

e. Sources of foreign currency

f. Prevents landslide and soil erosion.

g. Provides Oxygen and fresh air.

h. Helpful to agriculture.

i. Maintain environmental balance.

What are the causes and consequences of environmental pollution ? Suggest the remedial measures to correct it.

The causes of environmental pollution are:

a. Rapid population growth.

The size of the population in developing countries is growing rapidly. As the population increases, they demand more facilities which hamper the resources.

b. Growing deforestation.

The easiest way to solve the problem of needs of a human being is to use forest resources near them. They can earn money by selling timber, herbal product and fire wood.

c. Inadequate public awareness

Most people in rural areas are still uneducated. Uneducated people don't know about advantages and disadvantages of environmental resources.

d. Migration

The rapid growth of migration from hill and mountains to the Terai and city area has has put pressure on environmental health.

e. Lack of resource utilization.

Since developing countries are very poor in the field of science and technology, the government as well as civil society are unable to reutilize some renewable resources.

The consequences of environmental pollution are:

a. Water pollution

Water resources are being polluted due to mix-up of industrial waste and drainage with drinking water Pipes, which is responsible for water borne diseases.

b. Atmospheric Change

The unscientific use of available water, forest and minerals has resulted in so many problems in earth's surface.

c. Natural calamities

Rapid deforestation has resulted In uneven, unnatural, irregular and scarcity of rainfall, which leads to flooding, landslide, soil erosion etc.

d. Air pollution

Air pollution from vehicles and industries have resulted into air-borne diseases like hypertension, lungs problem and high

blood pressure.

e. Sound pollution

The sound pollution has adversely affected the life of Kathmandu, Pokhara, Birgunj and Butwal etc.

The remedial measures to correct environmental pollution are:

a. Control on population growth

Strict control over growing population by using curative and preventive methods would be the best solution to preserve the environment from being further polluted.

b. Development of public awareness

It is necessary to educate people about environment and it's important. They can analyses scientific use of different resources.

c. Introduction of new technology

The growing use of science and technology should be directed towards reutilization and recycling of used materials as much as it is possible.

d. Political Stability

A nation suffering from long term political instability cannot use its resources. Therefore long lasting government and political instability is essential.

e. Natural resource management plan

Since healthy environment is important to both public and private sectors. their effort must be directed toward the preservation of wildlife forest and other creatures.

Describe the importance of water resource.

The water is necessary for the life of every living beings. It is used for various purposes. Its importance are:

a. Development of agriculture

Irrigation can be provided. Commercialized development of agriculture entirely depend upon the development of a irrigation system in the country.

c. Development of industries

Hydroelectricity is considered as the cheapest energy. Generation of electricity helps industries to run smoothly upon the optimum capacity.

c. Development of transport & communication

Transportation and communication are the infrastructures required for rapid economic growth and development of a nation.

d. Development of tourism Industry

The tourism in Nepal has a close relationship with its natural setting. Sine rivers, rivulets, waterfalls, natural springs, lakes etc add to the natural beauty of the country. It would help to promote tourism Industry.

e. Preservation of forest resources

Firewood is the major source of  energy to the rural people of Nepal for cooking purpose. It fulfills about 75%t of national energy demand.

Describe the causes and consequences of deforestation in Nepal.

Deforestation has become the great challenge in the developing countries like Nepal.

Some of the major reasons are explained below:

a. Rapid population growth

The population growth of Nepal (2068) is 1.35% per annum. Large population demand more food, shelter and other basic facilities.

High dependency on firewood consumption

Firewood is most essential and the only alternative source of energy in rural life. Also, it is the cheapest Source of energy

b. Migration

Internal and external migration to improve their lives. They have to construct houses or shelters, land for cultivation farming, etc

c. Grazing of domestic animals

Most of the forests of hilly and terai region are adversely affected by grazing or domestic animals.

d. Frequent forest fires

Forest fires take place knowing or unknowing forest. Fire is still a very common phenomenon in rural parts of Nepal.

Consequences of Deforestation in Nepal

Deforestation adversely affects ecology & economic life of human society as well as other living species. Its affects are:

a. Environmental deterioration

Deforestation causes adverse effects on climate. The climate will be extremely hot in summer season and extremely cold in winter. It also invites irregular and abnormal rainfall etc.

b. Shortage of forest-based products.

Forest-based industries such as the match industry, paper industry herbal industry, etc are in danger of collapsing due to shortage of raw materials.

c. Decline in export earning

One of the major source of foreign currency earning of Nepal is the export of forest based products. Such as paper products, herbal products, wooden products and handicrafts.

d. Decline in underground water

The supply of underground water is determined by the availability of dense forests in the locality.

e. Instability of forest-based industries

The demand for forest products would increase due to increasing population.

chapters.title: Unit 10: Agriculture
chapters.content:
Describe the characteristics of Nepalese agriculture.

The characteristics of the Nepalese agriculture are:

a. Subsistence farming

b. Monsoon based agriculture

c. Dual ownership of land

d. Predominance of food crops

e. Traditional farming practice

f. Disguised unemployment

g. Small size of land holdings

h. Geographical variation.

i. Low productivity

j. Unequal distribution

a. Subsistence farming

It is one of the major characteristics majority of Nepalese involve in agriculture for their survival but they produce just enough for their own consumption.

Monsoon based agriculture

Agriculture in Nepal is dependent on the monsoon. Only 54% of total land has irrigation facility and rest 46% is completely dependent on monsoon rain.

d. Predominance of food crops

Food crops dominate the cropping pattern in Nepal. The share of food crops was around 50% share of cash crops was 28.1% & other 22.1%

e. Traditional farming practice

Nepalese farming practice is primitive as compared to other countries. Modem tools are not commonly used by farmers in the country.

f. Disguised environment

Agriculture is highly seasonal in nature and people are not employed all the year round. There are no alternative employment in rural areas.

Explain the importance of agriculture.

The importance of agriculture are:

a. Sources of food grains

b. Sources of industrial raw materials

c. Provides employment opportunities

d. Basis of foreign trade

e. Source of public revenue

f.Maintain environmental balance

g. Increase in the rate of savings capital formation & economic development

h. Supply of animal forage

i. Increase in living standard of the rural people

j. Sources of food grains

k. Main source of national income.

a. Sources of food grains

The agriculture sector fulfills the basic food requirements of the growing population. It provides various kinds of staple food crops, cash crops which are essential consumption for human life.

b. Source of industrial raw materials

Majority of industries of Nepal are agriculture based. The Agricultural sector provides raw materials like jute, grass, herbs etc

c. Provides employment opportunity

It provides opportunity to about 73.3% of the total working population of the country generates direct and indirect employment opportunities

d. Basis of foreign trade

Foreign trade in Nepal is mostly agriculture based Jute, tea , bones etc are the main exportable items of Nepal.

e. Sources of public revenue

Agriculture sector is regarded as one of the major sources of public revenue, the government generates its revenue through different types If taxes & fees

Describe the problems of Nepalese agriculture.

Although, agriculture is regarded as the backbone of Nepalese economy more focus for improving the sector has not been given The problems of Nepalese agriculture are:

a. Lack of irrigation facility

b. Lack of Agricultural Credit

c. Lack of storage facility

d. Lack of marketing facility

e. Use of traditional method

f. Defective Land tenure system

g. Defective Government policy

a. Lack of irrigation facility

Irrigation is regarded as the life blood of agriculture. No more land has irrigation facilities in Nepal. Besides modern techniques like double cropping & multiple cropping can’t be tried.

b. Lack of agricultural credit

Nepalese farmers need the credit time to time in order to undertake agricultural activities properly. Nepalese banks need to provide adequate loan to the needy farmers.

c. Lack of storage facility

There must be the modern storage facility to keep the products for long time to sell it at the period of more demand & high price. But, Nepalese farmers have no such facility.

d. Lack of marketing facility

Most of the farmers sell their products in unorganized market at low price due to lack of systematic marketing facility.

e. Use of traditional method

Nepalese farmers use very old fashioned. Inefficient tools and techniques are implemented in agricultural production. If these types of tools & implement are used then high agricultural product can't be realized.

Explain the remedial measures of problems Nepalese agriculture

Agriculture Sector faces serious problems despite the continuous efforts by the government for its development. Therefore, the following remedial measures should be applied to solve the Nepalese agriculture.

a. Control population growth.

b. Introduced land reform system

c. Provision of agricultural credit

d. Introducing modern farming

e. Providing irrigation facility

f. Developing agricultural markets

g. Adequate and regular agricultural research and extension work have to be carried out. All farmers should have access to such facilities

h. The government will have to adopt appropriate and effective policies for agriculture development

a. Control population growth.

Population pressure on agriculture land should be reduced by controlling the rapid growth of population and diverting agricultural labour to other sectors of the economy.

d. Introducing modern farming

Modern farming techniques are needed to introduced among the farmers. Improved seeds, chemical fertilizers and modem equipments should be made easily.

e. Providing Irrigation facility

Irrigation facilities have to be extended through out the country wherever possible. Adequate irrigation facilities ensure crop diversification as well as round the year forming.

f. Developing agricultural markets

Agriculture marketing facilities should be developed and provision of warehouse facilities should be made available in areas of the country.

chapters.title: Unit 4: Meaning and Indicator of Economic Development
chapters.content:
Comparison between economics Economic development And Economic growth.

Characteristics of Developing countries.

The countries which have low per capita income compared to the developed countries and the process of economic development has started but not completed are called developing countries. This countries are also known as 3rd countries of world, under-developed countries, poor countries and backward countries. Most of the countries like in Asia, Africa & North America are developing countries. Some of the characteristics of developing countries are as follows:

a. Low per capita income

The per capita income of these countries is very low as compared to the developed countries. For eg, The per capita income of developing countries like Nepal, Bangladesh and Ethiopia is $862, $1190 & $590 respectively. Due to this, these countries are suffering from various economic problem like poverty, under utilization of natural resources etc.

b. Rapid population growth

These countries are also suffering from the demographic characteristics. In these countries the population growth rate is between 2-3% per annum. Due to this, high population growth these countries are facing the problems like poverty, unemployment, deforestation, social inequality etc.

c. Mass poverty

Mass poverty is one of the major characteristics of developing countries. Large number of population is under the various circle of poverty, they are unable to fulfill their basic needs. For eg 21.6% of total population in Nepal, 28.5% of total population in Bangladesh & 33.5% of population Ethiopia lives under the poverty line.

d. High dependency on agriculture

Agriculture s the prime occupation in the developing countries. More than 70% of the active labor force is involved in agriculture. Likewise agricultural sector has significant contribution in the GDP of country. For eg, the total percent, 66% of population is engaged in agriculture and its contribution in GDP is 29% in Nepal.

e. Dual Economy

In the developing countries, there is the existence of two sectors of economy i.e traditional & modern which is called as dual economy. Due to this majority of the people living in the remote areas follows the traditional farming or subsistence farming only for their livelihood but day few of the people living in urban area follow the modern farming.

Economic indicators

Indicators of economic development is defined as the changes which takes place in the process of development that shows the living standard of the citizen of a nation. The types of indicators are as follows:

a. Gross National Product (GNP)

b. Per Capita Income (PCI)

c. Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI)

d. Human Development Index (HDI)

e. Basic Needs / Requirements.

Regarding indicators of economic development there are different opinions of different Economists. However Some of the common and popular indicators are as follows:

a. GNP

GNP is one of the indicators of economic development. It means economic development can be measured in terms of increase in real national income of a country over a long period of time. Some of the Economists argue that real GNP is better indicator of economic development but it has foiled to take consideration of change in growth of population, pollution, distribution of income, etc. Therefore, it doesn't cover all the production of developing countries which ate produced only for consumption level.

b. Per Capita Income

PCI is the first and most important indicator of economic development. It refers to the national income divided by total population. So, it is the  average income of each Individual in an economy. The per capita Income (PCI) of least developed countries is less than $995. For eg, the PCI of Nepalese people is $862 (economic Survey 2016 /2017). It is also not satisfactory indicator of economic development because the rise in PCI mayn’t guarantee the living standard of people. The different classification is as shown below:

c. Physical quality of life Index

It is a non-income economic development indicator which was developed by Moris D, that consist of 3 indicators i.e. life expectancy, literacy rate and in-fact mortality rate. The value of PQLI is measured in a scale of 0-100. If the people live longer and are literates  its value crosses 50 and the country is supposed to be developed. If the value lies below fifty, the country is supposed to be developing.

d. HDI
